Investigation Reveals Who Betrayed Photographer Secretly Documenting Nazi-Occupied France

A new investigation has uncovered how a brave photographer, who risked his life taking hundreds of pictures of Nazi-occupied France, may have been betrayed by two neighbors.

In April 2020, a mysterious album containing hundreds of photos of daily life during the German Nazi occupation of Paris from 1940 to 1942 was discovered in a flea market in Barjac in Gard, France.

Raoul Minot.1940-42. Paris occupé WW2 pic.twitter.com/SBnUj87HWA

— Paris Paname (@ParisAMDParis) August 24, 2024

Le Monde journalist Philippe Broussard began a four-year investigation to identify the photographer, who had taken at least 700 pictures of Paris during the first two years of the Occupation. At the time, unauthorized photography was banned by the Nazis, and taking such pictures could carry the death penalty. In 2024, Broussard identified the photographer as Raoul Minot.

Minot used a “little Kodak Brownie 6/9 camera” and developed the prints in the photographic laboratory of the department store where he worked. He then sold hundreds of his images to the French Resistance, a collection of groups that fought against the Nazi occupation during World War II.

However, Minot’s photographic mission came to an end in November 1942, just two years after it began, when an unidentified informer reported his activities to the Nazis.

Minot was imprisoned and deported to Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria on April 20, 1943, where he was forced to perform labor. He was later transferred to Flossenbürg concentration camp in Bavaria and liberated by U.S. forces on April 23, 1945. He tragically died five days later in a hospital in Cham, Bavaria.

Following his discovery of Minot in 2024, Broussard set out to uncover who had turned in the photographer to the Nazis for a report in Le Monde. A breakthrough came in April 2026, when a reader contacted Le Monde with a document that could help solve the mystery. Jean-Pierre Gross, a local history enthusiast from Courbevoie, France, had discovered a 1944 report accusing two of Minot’s neighbors, Marie Breux and Georges Robinson, of collaborating with the Germans and helping secure the arrests of people suspected of opposing the Occupation.

The report specifically named Minot, stating that the couple were suspected of having “denounced or, at the very least, incriminated” him. It also claimed they had boasted about getting 18 people arrested.

Breux was the building’s concierge, while Robinson, her partner, was a tailor with a history of theft and other criminal convictions. Both were arrested following the Liberation in August 1944, although no record of a conviction against either has been found.

Further investigation revealed that Robinson had briefly worked at the same Printemps department store as Minot, potentially explaining how he knew about the store’s photographic facilities.

Broussard later uncovered an anonymous letter sent in December 1942 that accused Minot and his wife of photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage. The letter prompted a police investigation that led to Minot’s arrest and the seizure of more than 1,000 photographic negatives.

“Sir, could you ask the Minot household, both of whom work at the Printemps — the wife as a cashier, the husband as a warehouse manager — whether their jobs qualify them to take photographs of propaganda posters and air raid damage to our poor country?” the letter reads. “We don’t think it would be very useful to inform you about the troubled times France is going through, thanks to many workers in troubled waters.

According to Le Monde, a handwriting expert subsequently ruled out Robinson as the author of the anonymous letter that triggered the investigation into Minot, but could not exclude Breux. Broussard believes the couple may have worked together to report Minot after discovering that he was photographing Nazi propaganda posters and bomb damage around Courbevoie.

Although there is still no conclusive evidence to establish who sent the letter, Broussard’s investigation has brought researchers closer than ever to identifying the people who may have brought Minot’s secret photographic mission to an end.

#9053. Arkivism Is a Searchable Archive of More Than Four Million Free Public Domain Images

Arkivism Is a Searchable Archive of More Than Four Million Free Public Domain Images

A new website called Arkivism aims to make searching for historical imagery considerably easier by bringing more than four million public domain images and videos together in one place.

The free-to-use archive (requires sign-up) includes historical photography from the Library of Congress, NASA imagery, and vintage film reels. Users can search the collection using natural language, describing what they want to find rather than having to know the exact title or filename of an image.

Arkivism also has an interface that will feel familiar to Pinterest users, with an infinite scroll, visual discovery features, and the ability to save images and videos to personal boards. Users can also extract high-resolution stills from archival video clips.

According to its creator, James, the archive currently contains more than four million full-resolution images and over 27,000 searchable film clips. Each asset also includes a backlink to its original source.

“Arkivism started as a fix for my own problem,” James tells PetaPixel, who explains that he used to edit long-form video documentaries on YouTube for the channel History of the Earth.

“There are millions of incredible public domain assets out there, but they’re scattered across slow, dated archives. Unless you knew the exact filename, finding one specific image could take hours. I wanted one place where I could describe what I needed in plain English and search everything at once.”

The project has been developed independently in James’s spare time since July. Despite its size, Arkivism is largely a one-person operation, with AI coding tools helping to make the development process more manageable.

James says the biggest challenge has been building systems capable of collecting material from numerous online sources while ensuring that every asset is properly validated as public domain.

“Above all, every asset has to pass validation checks confirming it’s public domain, because that’s the whole point of the site,” he says.

That emphasis on historical material is also part of the motivation behind the project. With AI-generated imagery becoming increasingly prevalent online, James believes there is particular value in making authentic historical photographs and footage easier to discover.

“I’m not anti-AI, obviously, but there’s real value in looking back, and I think that’s where the site really shines: you can dive endlessly down historical rabbit holes,” he says.

Although Arkivism borrows some of its interface design from Pinterest, James sees it as both a searchable archive and a visual discovery platform. Unlike traditional institutional archives, users can browse the collection without necessarily knowing what they’re looking for. Unlike Pinterest, however, the experience is not driven by an algorithm and contains no advertising.

“The site and archive will stay free,” James adds. “But further down the line I plan to build optional paid tools, such as After Effects and Figma plugins that bring the archive straight into editing software.”

The intended audience extends beyond photographers and filmmakers. Researchers, designers, and anyone looking for historical imagery can use the platform to find and download material, with the reassurance that assets have been checked for public domain status.

Arkivism is available now at Arkivism.com.

#9049. The astonishing, untold story of Marie-Anne “Baby” de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, who smuggled a Van Gogh painting and the artist's letters out of Nazi Europe

Marie-Anne “Baby” de Goldschmidt-Rothschild (1920s)

Photograph by Ernst Schneider, Laure de Margerie collection

Adventures with Van Gogh is a weekly blog by Martin Bailey, The Art Newspaper's long-standing correspondent and expert on the Dutch painter. Published on Fridays, stories range from newsy items about this most intriguing artist, to scholarly pieces based on meticulous investigations and discoveries.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

Among the early Van Gogh collectors was a young woman who had just turned 22. Born in 1892 to a very wealthy German family, Marie-Anne (nicknamed “Baby”) de Goldschmidt-Rothschild certainly had the money, but also avant-garde taste. She bought one of the artist’s finest portraits.

Her amazing story is told in a meticulously researched new book: A Collector’s Odyssey: How Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild saved her Paintings from Nazi Looting, written by Christel Force, Anna-Carolin Augustin and Katharina Weiler and published in Berlin by De Gruyter (it is freely downloadable).

Van Gogh’s The Arlésienne (November 1888)

Musée d’Orsay, Paris (Donation sous réserve d'usufruit Mme R. de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, 1952 © photo : RMN-Grand Palais (Musée d’Orsay) / Stéphane Maréchalle)

It may come as a surprise that the very first painting bought by Marie-Anne (whose maiden name was Friedländer-Fuld) was a Van Gogh - and an important one. Encouraged by progressive mentors, in June 1914 she purchased The Arlésienne (November 1888), a portrait of the artist’s friend Marie Ginoux, co-owner of the Café de la Gare in Arles. The picture cost the equivalent of £6250, a very large sum for a Van Gogh at the time. (There is another version at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art)

Marie-Anne later recounted how she hung the portrait, on antique-gold wallpaper, in her suite in the family’s palatial residence in Berlin’s Pariser Platz, almost next to the Brandenburg Gate: “My first and only painting, at the centre [of her main room], dominating everything and everyone, was L’Arlésienne by Van Gogh”. Her father, who had much more traditional tastes, abhorred the artist, telling her to hide “the jaundiced old lady” behind a curtain.

Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild, with her Louis XV sofa and Van Gogh’s The Arlésienne in her Berlin mansion (1929)

Photograph by Ernst Schneider, De Querschnitt journal (Berlin), September 1929

This was only the beginning. Marie-Anne went on to collect other Impressionist artists and their followers: Paul Gauguin, Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edouard Manet, Paul Cezanne and Pablo Picasso.

By the time Marie-Anne was 31, she had married three times: to the English aristocrat John Mitford, the former German foreign minister Richard von Kühlmann and the aristocratic banker Rudolf von Goldschmidt-Rothschild (he used “von”, while she preferred “de”). After a few years, she and Rudolf lived independently and eventually divorced in 1938.

With the rise of the Nazis, Marie-Anne, who was of Jewish heritage, smuggled the Van Gogh portrait twice. The first time was in 1934, a year after Hitler came to power, when she secretly sent the painting from Berlin to her residence in Paris. This required subterfuge: she commissioned an artist friend, Eugen Spiro, to paint identical copies of her most important paintings. The copy of The Arlésienne was then surreptitiously placed in the frame in her Berlin mansion, with no one apparently noticing the switch.

The Van Gogh and the other canvasses were taken off their stretchers and rolled up. Marie-Anne instructed Marie-Anne instructed her (female) servants to each carry a single roll to Paris, without telling them what was inside. Had the pictures been declared at the border, Nazi officials would have prevented them from being exported or would have charged her an exorbitant tax. The Arlésienne safely arrived at Marie-Anne's mansion in Paris on the Rue de la Faisanderie.

Six years later, France was threatened by Germany. In mid-May 1940, a month before the Nazi occupation of Paris, Marie-Anne decided to flee to the US, protecting her life and collection. By that time, the only route was via Portugal, which was neutral. In a move which the book’s co-author Force describes as “reckless and admirable in equal measure”, Marie-Anne hatched a plan for her most important paintings.

She took the canvases strapped to the roof of her Citroën. Amidst the chaos of millions fleeing Paris, she drove across France to Spain, facing seemingly endless logistical challenges, but eventually reaching Portugal. Although some reports suggest the Van Gogh was transported on the roof with the rest of the paintings, Marie-Anne later told a different story.

According to her, The Arlésienne had been sent earlier to Amsterdam, on loan for an exhibition. Just one week before the German invasion in May 1940, her contact in the Netherlands somehow managed to get the Van Gogh onto an aircraft bound for Lisbon.

In her hotel room in Portugal, Marie-Anne rolled up all her paintings, although the thick impasto paint of The Arlésienne created problems. She then covered the whole roll with a protective tarpaulin. Eventually she secured a place on a liner crossing the Atlantic, bound for Mexico.

After her ship finally arrived at Veracruz, Marie-Anne travelled on to Mexico City, later taking a plane to Texas and another flight on to New York, accompanied by her paintings. The Arlésienne had been travelling during wartime for nearly five months, arriving in New York in November 1940.

Marie-Anne, thanks to her immense wealth and elite contacts, had managed to escape the terrible fate of the vast majority of continental European Jewry.

In 1928, Marie-Anne made another prescient purchase: a collection of 22 letters written by Van Gogh in 1887-89 to his artist friend Emile Bernard (plus one to Gauguin). The bulk of Vincent’s surviving letters remained with Theo and his heirs, so the Bernard correspondence represented a very important acquisition. Many of the letters also included small sketches of the paintings which Van Gogh was working on.

Van Gogh’s letter to Emile Bernard, around 19 June 1888 (extracts)

Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam (Vincent van Gogh Foundation)

When the art lover and writer Harry Kessler visited Marie-Anne in 1929, he noted in his diary that they had dined under The Arlésienne. Kessler then recorded: “After dinner, thirty letters by Van Gogh in an excessively ornate, ugly binding, were passed around with cigarettes and coffee.” (Although Kessler said it was 30 letters, it was actually 23.) Contrasting the opulence with the artist’s simple way of life, Kessler added: “Poor Van Gogh!”

In 1940, when Marie-Anne fled from Paris in her Citroën, she carried this ornately-bound volume of Van Gogh’s correspondence in a suitcase. She kept the letters during her American wartime exile.

On 26 August 1944, just hours after Paris was liberated, Marie-Anne wrote from California to the Free France delegation in Washington, DC: “My hand is shaking with emotion as I am writing to you today, day of the Liberation of Paris. I turn to you to ask that whoever is concerned be informed that I bequeath my Van Gogh painting L’Arlésienne to the city of Paris. It is at the Louvre, I expect, that it will find its place.”

Marie-Anne left New York and returned to Europe in 1947, once again taking her paintings with her. Her family’s palatial residence in Berlin had been almost totally destroyed by Allied bombs, and she wanted to settle in her mansion in Paris. There she would spend the rest of her life, until her death in 1973.

The dining room in Marie-Anne de Goldschmidt-Rothschild’s Paris mansion (1950s)

Photograph by Antoinette Georges Perrier, De Goldschmidt-Rothschild family archive

Marie-Anne had lived with The Arlésienne for nearly 60 years. After her death, the painting went to the Louvre, which displayed it in the Jeu de Paume. It was transferred to the Musée d’Orsay when it opened in 1986.

We can report that next year The Arlésienne will be presented in an exhibition at the Musée de l’Orangerie in Paris: Dépossédes: Oeuvres spoliées, vies brisées 1933-45 (Dispossessed: Plundered Art, Shattered Lives 1933–45)(October 2027-January 2028). Marie-Anne’s life certainly had its challenges, but it was hardly shattered like most of the other collectors who will be featured in the show.

As for the Van Gogh correspondence, Marie-Anne donated one letter to the Fondation Custodia in Paris, another somehow left her collection and the one addressed to Gauguin was given to a friend. This left 20 letters which she bequeathed to her grandson, Frédéric de Goldschmidt-Rothschild. He sold the group to the New York dealer and collector Eugene Thaw in 2001.

Thaw later recalled how he bought the letters: “A young man [the grandson] showed up in my office with them all under his arm—unframed, unmatted—in a simple folder. And of course I nearly died of pleasant shock at seeing them.” Marie-Anne’s ornate binding had already gone.

The correspondence was generously donated by Thaw to New York’s Morgan Library & Museum. These important Van Gogh letters, with their 14 sketches, are now reunited online with the rest of the artist’s correspondence.

For conservation reasons, Van Gogh's letters to Bernard are very rarely exhibited, but I once had the privilege of examining the originals in the Morgan’s study room. Seeing the letters, penned by the artist on ordinary writing paper with his little sketches, I thought back to when they had once been housed in Marie-Anne’s ornate album—and their perilous journey during the war.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#9045. Eight furniture designs informed by life in New York City

Furniture designers contend with their personal experiences living in New York City through the objects in our most recent roundup.

New York, New York has inspired filmmakers, writers and artists to make work since the city’s inception, and for designers, it’s no different.

The furniture and objects below explore aspects of moving to or living in New York City, whether it’s the difficulty of maintaining a career and community, the dissonance of missing home, the architecture, or dead, smooshed rats on the daily commute.

In many cases, the collections reflect on the designer’s own identities and heritages.

These include pieces by Kim Mupungilaï, Rafael Prieto and studio Tian & Teague, all of whom have lived or passed through New York during their practice.

Read on below to see how the metropolis has shaped their work.

Bechara Maalouf created a series of lamps made out of wooden beams from Lower East Side buildings and intricate screens informed by the window guards at his family home in Lebanon.

The series, first displayed during NYC design week 2026 in May, merged Maalouf’s two homes as the designer grappled with the impacts of Israel’s ground invasion of Lebanon from afar.

Designer Massimiliano Malagò created an acrylic chair, covered in his own writings, that explores the challenges of maintaining a life in New York City.

“For me, this was making an object that is incredibly luxurious, incredibly grand, but it’s actually talking about something quite common and sometimes quite sad, because the hardships that people go through to stay in the city are just difficult,” he told Dezeen.

Los Angeles and Lisbon studio Tian & Teague created the NYC Series based on their own time living in New York and some of the jarring aspects residents become accustomed to.

The collection, which includes a flattened-rat rug, came about from things seen on the studio founders’ daily commute.

New York-based designer Han Seungmin created this chair using modular components from the metallic fences found throughout Brooklyn.

First mass-produced in China in the 1980s, the fences are often used in Asian communities around the boroughs, and Han challenged “the idyllic image of the ‘American Dream’ from an immigrant perspective” through the piece.

Belgian interior designer Kim Mupungilaï was prompted to design this collection of wood and fibre furniture after a 2018 visit to New York that inspired her to explore her half-Belgian, half-Congolese roots.

“I just started thinking about my own cultural landscape and background and upbringing and wanted to dig deeper,” Mupungilaï told Dezeen.

Metalworker and designer Micah Rosenblatt looked to New York City’s historic architecture for his The City Block collection, which features thin, contemporary lines and geometric elements.

“[The expressions] are based on the cityscape and my relationship to it,” Rosenblatt told Dezeen. “It’s the forms that you would look out and see on your horizon via whatever time period you’re in.”

All Other Passports, by Julio Torres and Sabai

Comedian and actor Julio Torres worked with furniture company Sabai to create his first furniture collection, All Other Passports, debuted during NYC design week 2026.

The collection is influenced by literal and figurative aspects of Torres’ move to New York City from El Salvador, such as a curtain motif pulled from JFK‘s international Terminal 4.

Find out more about All Other Passports ›

For The Future of the Past, by Rafael Prieto

Designer Rafael Prieto integrated building fragments into several furniture pieces for an exhibition at Emma Scully Gallery earlier this year.

Prieto sourced the cast-offs, including pieces of a cornice, from a facade being demolished across the street from his Tribeca studio, which he had become “deeply interested” in.

#9044. Black (and White) Film Friday: There are Over 45 Emulsions to Explore

Black (and White) Film Friday: There are Over 45 Emulsions to Explore

It is our largest (and most fun) Film Friday of the year: Black (and White) Film Friday! While our Film Fridays tend to spotlight a single emulsion, with this annual celebration we feature the entire selection of black and white film stocks that we have in our inventory. But before we dig in too far, it would be a good moment to explain our inspiration for Film Friday.

This story is brought to you by Blue Moon Camera and Machine in Portland, OR. Blue Moon offers film, development services, printing, and even an ever-rotating line of film cameras and lenses.

PetaPixel Members receive 10% off all lab services with Blue Moon: Join today!

Blue Moon Camera and Machine launched Film Friday publicly in 2019, but it had been an ongoing project of ours for several years prior to that. The film that started it all was Ilford XP2. See, we (the collective “we”, that is, as in all of us film photographers) have always had an amazing selection of films to choose from as we decide what to load in our cameras. This selection has evolved over time. Some years it has winnowed down, and other years it has actually expanded. But there have always been just so many films out there to make our work and art with. It is also true, however, that most of us gravitate to certain films. We find the emulsion we like, and we settle into it.

This is neither a good behavior nor a bad one—perhaps it is both; it is simply what we tend to do. And even when you work in an all-analog camera store, like Blue Moon Camera, you can fall into these patterns. And this is where XP2 comes in. Ilford XP2 was one of those films we never used all that much. To be honest, Kodak Tri-X and Ilford HP5 were our typical go-to film stocks. Yet every now and then we would find cause to shoot with a roll of XP2 instead.

This might happen two or three times a year. And each of those times we would get the negatives back and think to ourselves, “Wow, XP2 is a gorgeous film. Why don’t we use this stuff more often?” Of course, the answer is because we know what we know, and we like to stick with that. And thus we decided to set about changing this. We made it a personal project to not just shoot a roll of every film we carried, but actually use it repeatedly and get to know it. One film at a time we would go out for several months, working through multiple rolls, taking our time, learning each emulsion’s quirks and characteristics, and then coalescing those experiences into a collection of images and a written review. The goal was to pass along not just the knowledge and experience we had gained, but the inspiration as well.

There is something to be said for working in depth and committing to a single film and knowing it like you know nothing else. But there is also something to be said about breadth and being familiar with all the myriad options open to you in your creative pursuits. And that is the beating heart of our Film Fridays. It is about celebrating the wealth of options open to us. It is about reminding ourselves that there are more films out there than simply Ultramax, Portra, or HP5. And of course, it is about learning and growing as film photographers.

So having said all that, we came up with the idea of Black (and White) Film Friday only a few years ago. Yes, it is timed to coincide with Black Friday, and yes, quite admittedly, there is a bit of a commercial gimmick built into that. But there is also more to our B&W Film Friday than the sales angle. Let us explain.

In a similar way to how many of us gravitate toward a select few film stocks, we have also noticed that, generally speaking, many film photographers lean toward color film photography. This is especially true with newer film photographers. A big reason is we see the world, and our lives, in color, so it is a natural or even reflexive deduction to photograph with color film. Time and again we have had customers at the counter ask for film recommendations, and we, in turn, ask if they are interested in color or B&W film. It is not uncommon for them to respond to that simple question with some surprise that they had not even considered black and white and had never even tried a roll of it. This is the thing with habits; they tend to fit so snugly we can forget they are even there.

But B&W film should not be forgotten or overlooked. In short, there is a classic beauty and a timelessness that can only be captured with B&W film. It also simplifies the world in its way by converting colors that may otherwise be distracting into tones of grey and letting us make images about something other than the reds, oranges, yellows, greens, blues, and violets of the world.

Black and white allows us to focus on light, textures, relationships, shapes, patterns, grit, grain, and so many other elements (or ideas). It isn’t that you cannot do these things with color film—you can—but there is a directness with which B&W lets you approach these things. This is harder to understand via explanation than it is through experience. So we run our B&W Film Friday not just for the photographers who already love their black and white films, but also for those who have never stepped into those waters.

And there is a crazy variety out there to work with. There are more different types of black and white films than there are color films. We did a rough count, and once you eliminate all the different format choices and focus on just the different emulsions, we have at least 45 unique film stocks to try.

These films are mostly of the black and white negative type, but there are a few reversal films as well and also a couple of black and white instant films to keep in mind. Let’s repeat that number for emphasis: there are at least 45 unique black and white films in our inventory alone. And we don’t even carry every possible B&W film option on the market. That is easily in the 50s and maybe the 60s once you go out into the wider market looking for these films.

So what are you waiting for? That is a lot of film to try, and our guess is most of you have perhaps not even used half of these. So take advantage of this one day where you can pick up more of your favorite B&W film, or you can try something entirely new. We heartily recommend doing both. Visit our online store or come by our shop in St. Johns, Portland, Oregon, and get some film.

#9042. Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them,” he continued.

“That fusion is at the heart of this project – how do these technologies, through cultural practices on the ground, begin to morph into new creatures and new constellations that people try to make sense of to interpret the violence of this military technology that is taking place.”

Nahleh and Saloojee aimed to combine the reality of modern war with mythical storytelling, drawing upon their research into communities exposed to military attacks.

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures – creatures that fuse together technological advancement with epistemic practices and myth-making practices that happen from the ground,” said Nahleh.

“Most of these creatures, these modern constellations as we’re calling them, are populating the night sky in our drawing alongside pathways of flights of drones, satellites and other things that manifest across the night sky we’ve inherited, rather than the one we lost,” he continued.

“We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us, be it in the shape of missiles, phosphorus, or flares.”

As well as depicting creature-like constellations in their inner curves, the structures themselves were designed as creatures – the nocturnal Solifugi spider known to run out the sun and into shade.

“The project is dedicated to the Solifugi, which is a spider that by nature runs away from the sun, the sun of imperial savagery,” said Nahleh. “It has a very thick skin to protect it from this brightness, and in its belly is a map of the contemporary sky.”

Three openings puncture the shell in each of the installations. In the desert site at Al Madam, a vertical cut-out frames a view of the minaret of a distant mosque, and at the slaughterhouse site, a long opening was set at the height of a cow.

Traditional Hakawati storytellers will narrate stories at the installations as part of the triennial, which runs until April.

“The story is difficult, but it’s about finding optimism,” said Nahleh. “People are carving their own histories on the weapons that are here to annihilate them.”

“There’s a paradox here that we have to confront,” he continued. “When libraries are being erased, and people have no more books to publish or things to write on, they’re writing on the weapons that are sent to devour them.”

“Kids now are finding ways again to dream by placing their wishes upon the shooting stars, which are usually missiles and rockets. It’s a sad and complicated story, but we can no longer escape it by wishing for a sky we no longer have.”

We rounded up eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which includes a draping shelter that pays homage to the improvised learning spaces created by Virginia’s Black community, and a circular canopy with cut-outs that plot 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun.

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#9039. Even if the Nikon D850 Is Discontinued, It Won’t Be Hard To Buy

Even if the Nikon D850 Is Discontinued, It Won’t Be Hard To Buy

The Nikon D850 may be on its last legs, but that doesn’t mean photographers can no longer get their hands on one.

Nikon Rumors reports that Nikon’s Sales Support team in the United Kingdom communicated that the Nikon D850 is “now end of life,” which effectively means it is discontinued.

“We would like to inform you that the D850 model is now end of life. Unfortunately, we are not expecting any further stock, and as a result, we are not accepting new orders. Please update your systems accordingly. We apologize for any inconvenience. If you have any questions, please let us know,” Nikon’s UK Sales Team said in an email.

This aligns with the UK retail situation, where stock varies by retailer. For example, Wex, a major UK photo retailer, no longer lists the D850. However, as Digicame-Info reports, the D850 is still available in Japan, and it remains easy to find in the United States as well.

There are a couple of caveats here. First, as PetaPixel has seen plenty of times, cameras and lenses are often discontinued in one region before another. Second, nothing may have actually changed regarding Nikon’s manufacturing of the D850. The company could have halted production a while ago, and local stock has only just run dry in the UK, prompting the new notice.

PetaPixel has reached out to Nikon for clarification and will update this story when more information becomes available.

In the meantime, photographers can still acquire the Nikon D850. Even if new stock runs out, this prolific DSLR is widely available on the used market.

As for brand-new units, they remain readily available in the United States. B&H still carries the Nikon D850, for instance, and has it discounted by $300 through November 29 for the holidays. Nikon USA also still sells the D850 directly.

The Nikon D850 remains a fantastic camera that photographers still love, and it will stay easy to buy for the foreseeable future. The only real question is how much longer it will be available brand-new in the box—a status that will eventually end everywhere, not just in the UK.

#9038. Comment | The future of the ancient city of Palmyra should be determined by its local community

The Syrian antiquities department’s efforts to restore Palmyra—a Unesco World Heritage Site since 1980—are progressing again

The ancient city of Palmyra in Syria rose to the world’s attention in May 2015, when Isis militants occupied the site. Within five months, they had destroyed the Temple of Baalshamin, the Temple of Bel, and the Arch of Triumph—all 2,000-year-old masterpieces. That same year, their murder of Khaled al-Asaad, Palmyra’s retired head of antiquities, sparked worldwide outrage.

In the wake of these atrocities, institutions and governments around the globe launched a dizzying array of projects. Many focused on preserving the site digitally: the University of California San Diego Library reconstructed the Temple of Bel, for example, and the Université de Lausanne did likewise for the Temple of Baalshamin. Others aimed to one day physically reconstruct what had been lost, including a Russian project to restore the Arch of Triumph. But by the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, none of these plans had been realised.

Now under a new government, the Syrian antiquities department’s efforts to restore Palmyra—a Unesco World Heritage Site since 1980—are again progressing. It has been working to remove illegal constructions and stop illegal excavations, while Palmyra’s local community has been engaged in cleaning the museum’s gardens, among other projects. Meanwhile, a Heritage for Peace project is evaluating the structural condition of buildings in Palmyra’s modern city, which had a pre-war population of 70,000. This renewed momentum once again raises an important question: to what extent should Palmyra’s ancient ruins be physically reconstructed, if at all?

Archaeologist Nour A. Munawar of the University of Amsterdam addressed this problem in 2017, while the war still raged. He emphasised that whether or not to reconstruct should be a decision for Palmyra’s local community, irrespective of where they now live or their political views. Writing in Ex Noxo Journal of Archaeology, he warns that previous reconstruction projects largely left communities out of discussions—such as the limited local consultation when the Stari Most bridge was rebuilt in Mostar, Bosnia and Herzegovina, or how commercial buildings dominated the reconstruction of post-war Beirut. There is also the danger of “Disneyfication”, a label for artificial, over-polished reconstructions.

Whether to reconstruct has long been a dilemma for war-ravaged places. I recently visited Ypres, Belgium, a city that was totally destroyed during the First World War. In the aftermath, some wondered whether it should be rebuilt as it once appeared, or if its old architecture should be replaced with something more modern. Winston Churchill was in favour of leaving it untouched, as a memorial to the horrors of war. In the end, the local people made the decision: they wanted their Medieval town rebuilt—even if, for the most part, only the facades reflected the pre-war era.

A 2024 study by Benjamin Isakhan, a professor of international politics at Deakin University, Melbourne, and Lynn Meskell, a professor of anthropology at the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, provides an insight into how Syrians feel about this issue. After surveying 1,600 Aleppo residents, they found that almost all were proud of their cultural heritage, but Aleppines prioritised “safety and security”, “electricity, water and other services” and “unemployment and poverty” over “heritage protection and reconstruction” in terms of urgency.

And although 98% agreed that damaged or destroyed heritage sites should be restored or reconstructed, opinions varied on how: 17% wanted them to appear as “first built”, 24% as they appeared before the war, and 30% wanted them “restored and reconstructed into a new and more modern structure”. Heritage experts’ preference for authenticity could therefore go against some local wishes. Overwhelmingly, Aleppines also wanted Syrian control over rebuilding their heritage, not global agencies, NGOs, and foreign governments, Isakhan and Meskell note in the International Journal of Heritage Studies.

Palmyra is now a symbol of Syria, known worldwide. But whether the city’s rebuilt heritage retains its battle scars, becomes “Disneyfied”, or something in between, should be a local choice, as should whether any reconstruction is prioritised over more pressing needs. As time passes, an increasing number of voices will come into play—the new Syrian government, foreign governments, international bodies, NGOs and cultural heritage experts—all providing much-needed money, aid and advice. We must hope that the local community is not lost in the mix. In the end, it must be the people of Palmyra who decide their city’s fate.

#9037. Mondaine turns solar technology into design feature with Doppio Solar Skeleton timepiece

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” said Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

#9036. PGYTECH RetroVa Gives the iPhone a 400mm Reach and a Real Camera Feel

PGYTECH RetroVa Gives the iPhone a 400mm Reach and a Real Camera Feel

PGYTECH is best known for camera bags, tripods and straps, and in the phone world for telephoto extender lenses designed for Vivo and Oppo flagships. Its RetroVa kit brings that lens work to the iPhone.

The system first appeared on Kickstarter in January 2026 for the iPhone 16 Pro and 17 Pro families, combining a camera-style Bluetooth grip, retro-style case, and a 2.35x teleconverter for the phone’s telephoto lens. The newest version designed for the iPhone 17 Pro/Pro Max and 18 Pro/Pro Max series brings in a lighter and smaller 2X lens, along with a 4X telephoto lens as an alternative.

This all provides focal range that simply doesn’t work as well when using the phone itself. With 200mm, 235mm, and 400mm equivalents, the iPhone can reach farther with more optical clarity. A dedicated app also offers old school film simulations and manual controls for composition to let you decide how you want your images to look.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set comes in Graphite Black, while the 4X lens, grip, and the case are also sold separately and in smaller bundles, offering users different ways to put the kit together.

RetroVa Black Friday deal: From November 19 to 30, the RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set (Graphite Black, iPhone 17/18 Pro Max) is 10% off, and PetaPixel readers can take an extra 10% off with code BYTEDDYK. Buy it on Amazon or directly from PGYTECH.

The Ultimate Gift Set brings them all together in the box: the 4X telephoto lens, a lens adapter bracket, lens pouch, RetroVa phone case, grip, a photography strap, and an Arca-Swiss compatible tripod collar for the lens. The case is polycarbonate and works with MagSafe, leaving the proverbial door open for additional magnetic accessories. Though it has a lip over the edges, you can still use the case with a screen protector on the phone itself.

The lightweight grip weighs 63 grams for the Pro and 65.4 grams for the Pro Max. It carries physical controls, a built-in microSD slot, and a standard 1/4-inch socket on the base for tripods and monopods. It slides into the phone’s USB-C port with a lock switch that holds it firmly in place, though it actually pairs and connects to the device via Bluetooth.

It’s important to get the right size because there are separate variants for the Pro and Pro Max. While the lens mount is the same on either build, you can’t slide a Pro grip into the Pro Max, for instance. That also goes for the case, which is the most integral piece because that’s what everything else in the kit attaches to. Fortunately, since the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro models share the same dimensions, you don’t need to worry about compatibility in that regard.

The shutter button functions a lot like a typical camera would: half-press to focus, press to take the shot, or hold it down for a burst. The zoom lever right under it can either skip between focal lengths in Vintage mode or adjust zoom more freely in the Standard setting. Below that is the control dial that you can choose to adjust exposure, ISO, white balance, or shutter speed. Lastly, the multi-function button acts as power on/off, switches modes, and sets up Bluetooth pairing. A small LED next to it indicates pairing and a solid connection.

The microSD card slot (UHS-I or UHS-II) underneath is another handy way to save excess photos or video, albeit with some key parameters. You can readily save RAW photos or 4K video to it, only you’re limited to HEVC-coded footage and max 120fps. Plug the grip into a laptop where you can then offload the content directly.

If you record in Apple’s Camera app, video automatically goes to the card when you use supported formats, while PGYTECH’s app supports more recording formats. Even third-party apps that can record to external storage can recognize the card, too.

PGYTECH also makes 62mm and 67mm filter adapter rings sold separately from the available kits. They’re not included in any of them, though will work just fine with any filters in those two respective sizes. Being a separate piece, you just slide out the lens adapter ring and bring in the filter adapter instead. There is no way to use a filter with the teleconverter lenses themselves, since the filter adapter covers the iPhone’s entire rear array.

PGYTECH designed the kit to work with a dedicated companion app called PGYTECH: Pro Camera & Editor. It’s free to download, only requiring iOS 17 or later to run. You do, however, need to be diligent about keeping it up to date because if you don’t, the app may lock you out of all the manual control settings. A pop-up notice stating that a subscription is required to unlock those pro features isn’t actually necessary. Update the app and that message disappears.

While there is an Auto mode available, Manual provides controls for exposure, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, tint, and filters, which you can then map to the grip by going to Settings->Hardware Settings. You will need to ensure the grip is on and once connected via Bluetooth, select RetroVa in the drop-down menu to pick what you want. At any point within that section, you can always look at tutorials on connecting the grip and a video FAQ as well.

Unless you explicitly make your own manual adjustments, the app’s camera interface treats everything as if it was in Auto. So, shutter speed, ISO, white balance, and tint will all dynamically shift based on what’s in frame. Tap to focus works just like any other camera app would. One difference, though, is if you have Focus Assist on (focus peaking by another name), you will see where the camera is actually focusing after you tap, giving you an indication of where the focal plane is.

Other manual controls, like a histogram and priority facial recognition (the camera will always focus on a face first in this setting), are elective. Standard bits, like a timer, live photo, watermark, and aspect ratio (1:1, 4:3, and 16:9) round out much of what’s left. There is a Dive Mode that switches controls to physical buttons for underwater photos and video, while also applying an “underwater filter” as a copy of the original when captured. You can make separate manual settings adjustments for this mode, too.

In addition to about 15 standard filters, PGYTECH offers a series of nostalgic film simulations, ranging from Classic Negative and Nostalgic Negative to Kodak Gold 200, Fujifilm PRO Neg Std, Velvia 100, Classic Chrome, FujiColor C200, Tungsten 500, and Bleach Bypass. Choose any one at any time and adjust the intensity from 0-100. These simulations apply no matter what image format you shoot with and aren’t limited to still photos: they work with video, too.

The app includes a Retro Film mode that features the same set of film simulations, except it changes the hybrid zoom ranges to include 35mm and 50mm equivalents to better match traditional prime lenses. Otherwise, images process the same way as the Photo mode.

It’s also possible to apply any of these filters on a photo after you capture it within the in-app editing suite, including HSL for some color grading. Beauty features also present a variety of options for those seeking that kind of detail. Under Creative, there are templates for sharing or social media.

An on-device AI tool in the Adjust section lets you try enhancing detail in images by either using HD to improve clarity or AI HD to restore detail in softer images. You need to download it to make it work on-device rather than in the cloud but once it’s there, you can utilize it any time. If you’d rather avoid AI completely, you don’t have to use it.

Mind you, you’re not forced into PGYTECH’s app for basic shooting (without the lenses) since the grip also works with the native Camera app. To make that work with iOS, go to the Settings app, then Accessibility->Zoom->toggle On->Full Screen Zoom. At that point, having already paired it to the phone, you gain access to Apple’s own Camera app where pressing the shutter or zooming in responds onscreen. PGYTECH says it’s working on more third-party app integrations, so we’ll see where that leads.

The 4X lens is both the newest and the headline of the trio. It uses an 11-element, 3-group optical design with fluorite-grade low-dispersion glass and weighs about 137 grams. It feels sturdy in hand, which is why it’s smart to use it with the tripod collar when you need to prop it up for a long exposure or timelapse.

It’s a 400mm equivalent optical focal length, going up to 1200mm with a digital crop. The 4x lens also comes with a case and slightly different bracket that also includes a mount for the iPhone’s main camera. That gives you a 240mm optical equivalent or 400mm with an in-sensor crop with more background separation, which PGYTECH pitches for portraits.

The 2x lens, at about 104 grams, gives 200mm optical and 400mm cropped over the telephoto camera, or 105mm and 200mm over the main camera. This lens doesn’t come with a case but does include the same lens bracket the Ultimate Gift Set does, which only covers the phone’s telephoto camera. That’s an important distinction if you’re looking to use any of the lenses on both the main and telephoto cameras.

In the case of the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, the PGYTECH app can’t control the main camera’s mechanical aperture, so you can’t benefit from stopping down to f/4 for certain photo or video opportunities. Either way, all three lenses fit any of the RetroVa cases and brackets made for the iPhone.

One thing to always keep in mind is how much attaching the lenses considerably increases minimum focusing distance. PGYTECH lists 16.2 meters for the 4x over the telephoto camera and three meters over the main camera, against 5.22 meters and 60 centimeters for the 2x. There’s no optical image stabilization in any of them, so PGYTECH relies on its app’s stabilization algorithm for steadier handheld results. Handheld, the kit is better now than it was just a few months ago.

There’s nothing electronic communicating between the lenses and the app, so you have to manually select the lens you’re using and then turn that off or switch if you end up putting on another one. Doing so makes corresponding changes to available focal lengths and ensures focusing and processing fall in line with what you’re using. It’s one of the easiest things to forget while shooting with it in the field but it’s vitally important.

Technically, the lenses aren’t supposed to work with Apple’s own app, though I randomly found no obstruction in doing so. Other times, it didn’t work at all. This has nothing to do with the kit and everything to do with how Apple engineers its camera array. Because it functions as one virtual system, the software can decide what it thinks is the best camera, even though you’ve already chosen one over another. PGYTECH’s app doesn’t do that, leaning purely on whichever camera you’ve attached the lens to capture images or video.

If you get lucky enough to make Apple’s app work, it gives you access to manual controls (in the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max) as well as the possibility of manipulating the variable aperture with the main camera. It’s just a very hit-or-miss proposition, so your experience may truly vary.

As a kit, the RetroVa is trying to present a camera-like feel to capturing photos and video on the iPhone. That’s the basic gist, but in practice, the handling offers a fairly high degree of versatility in both perspective and ergonomics. Without having to stretch out a thumb or finger to hit the onscreen shutter, the grip’s controls make low or high-angle shots easier to manage. Double-clicking the iPhone’s Camera Control will launch Apple’s Camera app but if you prefer to switch that to PGYTECH’s app within iOS, go to Settings->Camera->Camera Control and tap on it to make that the default.

In the four months I’ve been using the kit (both with the iPhone 17 Pro and 18 Pro), multiple updates over that time have either added new features or refined existing ones. One thing you have to always remember is that this app processes images slower than Apple’s app does, especially when shooting in ProRAW. You can see that in the preview window where a yellow indicator shows that it’s rendering what you just shot.

The reason that matters is because it’s easy to ruin a photo by quickly moving the camera after capture. That very brief window between snapping the shutter and seeing the resulting image populate the preview window can feel like an eternity when shooting action, like I did at multiple WNBA games with this kit. It’s faster if you’re purely shooting JPEG or HEIF but the same thing can happen if you’re a little too eager to see what you just got.

Part of what PGYTECH is up against is the smaller 1/2.55-inch sensor Apple uses for the telephoto camera on both the 17 Pro and 18 Pro series. Adding significant optics to that lens certainly gets you closer to the subject or action but it’s best to also learn the subtleties of PGYTECH’s app. Lighting conditions are of paramount importance, as noise can creep in at higher ISO levels when you need to raise the shutter speed.

While you can shoot in either ProRAW, JPEG, or HEIF at either 12 or 48-megapixels, you don’t really wield any outsized control over the imaging pipeline. Apple’s processing engine still kicks in, forcing you to lean more on RAW images if you feel more comfortable with the higher degree of manual control available. PGYTECH isn’t necessarily only targeting seasoned mobile photographers with the RetroVa kit but it’s still worth dealing with the learning curve.

The controls include manual focus, with focus peaking as an elective option where you get to choose between red, green, or blue as the visual aid. It applies no matter if you’re tapping to focus manually or adjusting it in the slider. One key tidbit is tapping to focus doesn’t always work as you’d expect because focal length (even for the iPhone’s own lenses) behave natively. Within the app, there’s no fusion between them to enable, say, macro shooting at closer distances where the main or ultra-wide might step in to help the cause.

All that aside, the handling is a big part of the appeal here. As a slab device, the iPhone can prove tough to work with under different perspective and angles, so the grip turns it into something you can maneuver in more interesting ways. With a finger on the shutter and the ability to make granular adjustments with the dial, plus the strap to take off the weight, the creative possibilities certainly stand out.

Focusing is the biggest challenge because subject tracking isn’t the same as Apple’s own implementation, and you often still need to tap on the screen to hone in on what you want the composition to look like. One workaround for that is to get a separate screen primarily used for rear camera selfies as a way to wirelessly compose a shot when it’s hard to contort yourself to see the real time preview on the phone.

PGYTECH says it’s working on tracking autofocus and on controlling the iPhone’s aperture from the grip, which would address two key challenges in using the RetroVa kit. A universal lens adapter and further lens types are also on PGYTECH’s wish list, though no firm commitment.

For now, RetroVa is an iPhone-only system built around the Pro and Pro Max models, albeit with some nuances noted earlier. Not everything made for the iPhone 17 and 18 Pro series applies to what’s available for the iPhone 16 Pro series.

It’s also worth noting the kit isn’t a qualitative replacement for a mirrorless camera. The iPhone’s image sensors aren’t in the same league to begin with, but the app’s manual controls are far more extensive and the lenses a big upgrade over the awful hybrid crops the iPhone offers on its own. Compared to a bigger mirrorless, however, this kit is easier to carry, especially when you take off the lenses.

The RetroVa All-in-One Ultimate Gift Set is 10% off through November 30, plus an extra 10% with code BYTEDDYK, on Amazon and at PGYTECH.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Whether you're a musician who needs accurate monitoring, a designer who wants something better than AirPods for long editing sessions, or simply someone who loves quality audio, Linsoul IEMs make some of the best IEMs (in-ear-monitors) around.

But, other than the best budget IEMs, they usually don't come cheap, so when Black Friday comes around, it's the perfect time to pick up a bargain.

In this article, I've picked out the IEMs I think are most worth your money, running from budget single-driver sets to the best multi-driver IEMs under $500. Many are models I've tested myself, and all of them punch well above their price tags.

I just love this IEM. Billed as the world's flattest IEM, the Reference is built for people who want to hear exactly what's on the recording. Twin 10mm dynamic drivers in a horizontally opposed layout handle the bass, while two Sonion balanced armatures take the mids and a Knowles supertweeter covers the top end. It's the top pick in my best IEMs under $500 guide for a good reason.

This is Xenns Mangird's most premium IEM to date, and it doesn't hold back on hardware: two dynamic drivers and eight balanced armatures per side, split across a four-way crossover. As a result, you get to enjoy a wide, open soundstage with clear, airy treble and loads of detail, while the swirling, abalone-style resin faceplates mean that no two pairs look quite the same.

I'm a big fan of the Tea Pro, which I called "engagingly musical and beautifully built" in my review. Its dual 8mm dynamic drivers and six balanced armatures deliver a full, natural and lush sound, with a sub-bass presence that's always there without ever swamping the midrange. It's not the most analytical, but perfect to relax into for hours at a time.

On a tighter budget? The EW300 packs a lot of tech for the cash, combining three driver types in one compact CNC-machined shell: a 10mm dynamic driver for the bass and mids, plus a 6mm planar and a piezoelectric driver working together on the highs. Swappable nozzles let you tweak the tuning, and overall, the sound from this IEM is warm, punchy and forgiving.

Out of all of ZiiGaat's recent releases, the Horizon is my favourite, earning 8 out of 10 in my review. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with two Knowles balanced armatures and two planar drivers, producing a bright-leaning, detailed sound with an impressively spacious soundstage. If you can handle a lively treble, it's an absolute treat.

Launched in 2022, the original Cadenza is a bit of a legend, and it's still the perfect budget entry point into the world of IEMs. A single 10mm beryllium diaphragm dynamic driver, sat inside a 3D-printed resin shell, delivers a balanced sound with rich mids and clear treble, for a low, low price. Light, comfortable and a big step up from basic buds.

Released early this year, the Cadenza II builds on its predecessor with a new 10mm titanium-coated dynamic driver and Kiwi Ears' updated KARS 2.0 bass-tuning system. My review focused on its near-neutral sound and excellent build quality, which includes a CNC-machined aluminium faceplate. If you like your sound bass-heavy, look elsewhere, but if you seek an affordable all-rounder, you're golden.

Billed as the world's first MEMS + 1DD + 3BA tribrid IEM, the Halcyon pairs a MEMS driver, a type of tech also used in hearing aids, with a 10mm dynamic driver and three balanced armatures. When testing it for my review I loved its deep, rumbly sub-bass and well-judged treble; if your playlists lean bass-heavy, it really shines.

The Odyssey pairs a custom 10mm dynamic driver with three genuine Knowles balanced armatures: two full-range drivers for the mids and an ultra-high frequency tweeter. What makes it stand out is its bass: low notes hit like a subwoofer but stop quickly rather than lingering. That keeps the neutral midrange clean and uncluttered, with vocals that sound natural rather than plasticky.

This IEM is a collab between audio brand ZiiGaat and YouTube reviewer Zeos of Z Reviews. Its single 10mm diamond-like carbon (DLC) dynamic driver serves up a hefty 16dB bass shelf, with warm, rich mids and enough treble extension to stop things getting muddy. If you like your music to rumble, this is the one.

The Lush is ZiiGaat's take on a studio monitor and is designed for sound engineers and stage musicians. It pairs a 10mm dynamic driver with four balanced armatures via a three-way crossover, with the bass cut off at 200Hz so it doesn't bleed into the mids. Expect a neutral, coherent and versatile sound in a light, comfortable resin shell.

As the name suggests, Punch Audio is all about big, bold bass, and the Patada gives that tradition a refined twist. Combining a 10mm ceramic diaphragm dynamic driver with a MEMS driver for the top end makes for a smoother, more open treble than you might expect, alongside the usual low-end thump. This is still a basshead set, then, just a slightly more well-behaved one.

The KE4 uses two 10mm dynamic drivers in an isobaric subwoofer arrangement, paired with two balanced armatures through a three-way crossover. It was an early affordable take on the 'New Meta' tuning, and when I reviewed it, I found the bass hefty but the midrange the real star: rich, layered and never boxy or thin. It's comfortable and non-fatiguing to wear, too.

CrinEar's first production IEM, the Daybreak, arrived in 2025 and is built more for enjoyment than analysis. Its combines a dynamic driver, two balanced armatures and two micro-planar drivers in a 3D-printed resin shell with aluminium faceplates. If the Reference prioritises strict accuracy, the Daybreak goes for a more engaging, crowd-pleasing sound that works with pretty much any genre.

It's been a remarkable year for in-ear monitors, and Chinese brands, often lumped together under the "ChiFi "label, are a big reason why. Companies such as ZiiGaat, Kiwi Ears and Simgot are releasing new models at a dizzying pace, and they're no longer just competing on price.

We're seeing genuine innovation, from MEMS drivers to micro-planars, alongside a wave of collaborations with influential reviewers such as Z Reviews and HBB.

The upshot? Sound quality that would have cost a small fortune a decade ago is now available for less than a decent pair of trainers, and the gap with the big established brands keeps on shrinking.

#9034. Museum acquisitions round-up: a Simone Leigh monumental bronze and an atmospheric early Rothko

© Simone Leigh, courtesy Matthew Marks Gallery

The American Friends of the National Gallery of Australia bought this sculpture by Simone Leigh last year from Matthew Marks Gallery in New York. The monumental bronze, measuring 3.3m long and 1.5m tall, is named after the Nigerian American artist and actress Okwui Okpokwasili. It shows a reclining woman in a cast raffia skirt, exploring the resilience and cultural memory that merges the semi-abstract female form with the African vernacular. This cast is the second from an edition of two (with one artist’s proof). In 2022, Leigh became the first Black woman to represent the US at the Venice Biennale.

Untitled (wharf, Gloucester, Massachusetts) (1934) by Mark Rothko

Cape Ann Museum, Gloucester, Massachusetts

Christopher Rothko, the son of the artist Mark Rothko (1903-70), says that while his father thought “all art was inherently of its time”, sometimes “even with a master of abstraction like Mark Rothko, art can also be inherently of its place”. He is referring to this painting—an atmospheric early watercolour-and-gouache work depicting the harbour in Gloucester—which Christopher recently donated to the Cape Ann Museum from his private collection. Mark Rothko frequently summered on Cape Ann, painting alongside two other New York artists: his mentor, Milton Avery, and his friend Adolph Gottlieb. This painting is included in Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea—a touring exhibition currently on view at the Phillips Collection in Washington, DC (until 24 January 2027).

Arc-en-ciel no. 5 (1913-14) by Robert Delaunay

It may not be instantly recognisable, but the lilac spire behind the rainbow in this painting is the Eiffel Tower—the tallest building in the world when the work was painted by Robert Delaunay (1885-1941). The French artist was the husband of Sonia Delaunay, and in 1912 they co-founded the short-lived Orphism movement—an offshoot of Cubism that prized bright colours and geometric shapes. This vivid oil-on-canvas work, measuring 35cm by 40cm, is one of several variations of the composition and shows Delaunay moving away from strict geometry to a looser, more expressive and rhythmic style. The painting, which sold at Christie’s in 2025 for $317,500 (with fees) from the collection of Arnold and Joan Saltzman, was exhibited by the London-based dealer Willoughby Gerrish at Tefaf Maastricht in March—where the sale to the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, was initially agreed.

Only Gorky and Pollock of his peers has so far been catalogued

A new book by the art historian Ben Street attempts to demystify how we look at art and argues for reacting instinctively to what we see
