#9020. Comment | Cop31 may have faltered but, as grassroots initiatives in the art world and beyond remind us‚ all is not lost

This year's United Nations Climate Change Conference, known as Cop31, concluded with no deal on Sunday, 22 November, two days after it was set to close

In this monthly column, Louisa Buck looks at how the art world is responding to the environmental and climate crisis.

The fact that Cop31 failed to reach a final agreement on tackling climate change is obviously cause for grave concern. Despite the talks in Antalya, Turkey running over by two days as delegates struggled to achieve a consensus, they were ultimately derailed by the refusal by a group of oil producing states—led by Saudi Arabia and including Russia—to allow any mention of fossil fuel in the conference’s final agreement. This despite an agreement already made at Cop28 in 2023 to “transition away” from coal, oil and gas. As a result, more than 130 countries, including the European Union (EU) and the UK, refused to sign off a deal which omitted any reference to the main cause of climate change.

“We will not accept a Cop that greenwashes fossil fuel”, declared the EU representative Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, environment and energy, also stating that a climate pact which makes no mention of fossil fuel was “unconscionable” and “failed to meet the moment.”

Much of the art on display at Cop also seemed out of kilter with the urgency of the times. The centrepiece of the official CopArt programme, which was installed across the Cop site and curated by art advisor and contemporary art curator Nagihan Ozel, was an extensive installation of 18 mirror panels installed in the Green Zone and created by veteran artist Heinz Mack who has been making similar work since the 1960s. Other conspicuous pieces included Anselm Kiefer’s giant seascape bearing a pair of metal scales, Für Rabbi Löw (2010-12) and a forest made from recycled cardboard from Eva Jospin. Two monumental bronze sculptures by Belgian artist Koen Vanmechelen, one of an ape standing on a mirrored glass sphere balanced on a human thumb and another of a child struggling to hold an iguana, are described by the artist as “exploring our relationship with the natural world.”

Also on show in the Cop Green Zone and an especially jarring symbol of the deep schisms and incompatible agendas that characterised this latest Conference of the Parties were five animal sculptures created from discarded electronic and industrial defence waste materials. These were part of the “Upcycling a Future Vision” art collection launched by Aselsan, Turkey’s largest defence contractor to demonstrate its “commitment to a circular economy”, according to Turkish state-run media, as well as to celebrate the company’s 50th anniversary and “future of more efficient, innovative and sustainable production.” In a further irony, the defence giant—which is majority owned by the Turkish Armed Forces Foundation and produces electronic warfare technology and naval and air defence missile systems—was awarded a Green Transformation certificate from the Turkish authorities in tribute to its sustainability efforts. These apparently include a five-year road map to maximise energy, water and raw material efficiency whilst reducing carbon emissions and recycling 87% of total waste.

But amidst the chaos and anomalies within Cop some consolation can be gleaned from the fact that, while the oil-producing countries united to derail proceedings (undoubtedly spurred by the absence of an official US delegation and the Trump administration's overt hostility to the global fight to combat climate change), nonetheless 193 countries plus the EU remain committed to the Paris Agreement. Collectively these nations account for around 85% of global emissions. And while not wrapped up in a final deal, a number of significant agreements were made at Cop31 which included countries backing faster electrification and clean energy, drawing up measures to cut methane emissions and passing measures to protect the planet’s forests and oceans and strengthen support for communities impacted by climate change.

Beyond the Cop negotiating rooms, there are also glimmers of progress. In the UK greenhouse gas emissions have fallen by more than 50% since 1990 (although this much-vaunted statistic doesn’t include international aviation, shipping and imports and exports, which makes it more like 24%, according to the Office for National Statistics). Solar panels now provide 28% of Pakistan’s power while France and Denmark have announced roadmaps to phase out all fossil fuel by 2050, with Spain, Portugal and other countries planning to do the same. While these shifts often have as much to do with the fall in the cost of renewable technology and its resilience to market swings as a desire to hit climate goals; nonetheless an incremental frustration at the Cop consensus model means that countries are increasingly going it alone in naming what needs to be done and in identifying how they will tackle it.

Still from The People's Emergency Briefing (2026) featuring naturalist and presenter Chris Packham

Case in point was last Monday (16 November) when, as Cop31 was rumbling on, an important milestone was reached in the UK as Parliament debated a nearly 139,000 strong petition which called for the government to hold a UK-wide emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis. The petition had been generated by the National Emergency Briefing (NEB), a public information campaign consisting of an influential group of leading experts and fronted by the British naturalist and BBC TV presenter Chris Packham. It was asking for a “prime-time Covid-style briefing across all channels” which would be introduced by the Prime Minister and delivered by independent experts in order to spell out the extent and risks posed by climate change and nature loss, along with the action—both public and governmental—that needs to be taken. More than seventy members of parliament from across the political spectrum attended the three-hour debate which ended broadly in favour of the proposed televised emergency briefing, although not officially agreed. Speaking for the government, climate transition minister Katie White MP did go on record to state that she and her colleagues would meet with the leaders of the NEB campaign and “explore opportunities to work together”, and work on public engagement within the government's climate and nature security taskforce.

Just as Westminster was being galvanised by the NEB campaign, so too was the art world. Two days after the briefing debate, Tate Modern hosted a packed screening of The People’s Emergency Briefing, a 50-minute documentary film made by the NEB and presented by Packham. An articulate panel of nine experts starkly presented the urgent threats that climate and nature breakdown pose to food security, nature, the economy, national security and public health. This film, which anyone can freely register to screen, has been responsible for fueling much of the groundswell of both public and parliamentary support for the NEB’s petition. Since its release in April last year, The People’s Emergency Briefing has been shown more than 5000 times across myriad sectors and in venues large and small throughout the UK, from church halls, offices and hospitals, with many more scheduled for the forthcoming months. As Katie White declared at the Parliamentary debate, “a film has become a movement.”

However—with a few notable exceptions—the People’s Emergency Briefing has not had much airing in the art world. But now this seems set to change thanks to the art world environmental charity the Gallery Climate Coalition (GCC), who organised the screening and the following panel discussion. This was chaired by Frances Morris, the former director of Tate Modern and nowthe GCC's chair, speaking with artist Heather Ackroyd and Peter Lefort, the green futures network manager at the University of Exeter.

The screening of The People's Emergency Briefing at Tate Modern on 18 November 2026

Among the two-hundred strong audience of artists, including Cornelia Parker and Marcus Coates, academics and art workers from across both the public and commercial sectors, there emerged a strong determination to galvanise action. Many declared a commitment to lobby their MPs, to organise screenings of the People’s Emergency Briefing in their galleries and generally to be more courageous in both acting individually and collectively to help instigate what Peter Lefort compellingly described as “positive tipping points.”

As Lefort explained, these tipping points occur when cumulative changes in behaviour, policies, expectations and attitudes reinforce each other and gather momentum to accelerate change and achieve transformative impact. As politicians falter and our systems for joining forces globally become increasingly dysfunctional and inflexible, it now seems increasingly clear that these new forces for change—such as the NEB, with allied activist groups and screenings occuring across Europe—are coming from the grassroots up, and that the creativity of the art world needs to be applied to shift ossified, seemingly intractable structures and open up new ways of thinking.

After all, it was back in 2019 that, on the instigation of artist duo Heather Ackroyd and Dan Harvey, a procession of bell ringing artworkers headed by a woman wearing a coat of living grass and riding a white horse, occupied Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. The event from the Culture Declares Emergency movement inspired then-director Frances Morris to make the institution of Tate declare a climate and ecological emergency, helping set in motion an increased environmental awareness that is now common currency throughout the art world. In the words of one attendee at last week’s Tate Modern gathering, “we may be small compared to other sectors but we can be LOUD!” So now let’s brush ourselves down after Cop and make our voices heard, before it is too late.

#9019. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

#9018. HTA Design unveils "UK's largest council housing development"

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

“Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) announced the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

#9016. Argentina leads the way in repatriating Indigenous human remains, study says

The director of the Australian Museum, Kim McKay, and Koro Johnny Tuki, representing the Rapa Nui people, mark the handing over of remains of Indigenous people in July Photo: Louise Reily; © Australian Museum

Driven largely by Indigenous activism, the repatriation of ancestral human remains in Chile and Argentina is pushing museums, universities and scientific institutions to re-examine longstanding practices of collection, research and display. A recent study by the Chilean researchers Jacinta Arthur and Patricia Ayala suggests that the movement has opened a crucial ethical debate in both countries, with key differences: while Chile has handled repatriation campaigns on a case-by-case basis, Argentina has emerged as a regional leader since passing a law specifically tackling the issue.

“Argentina is central to any discussion of this issue in South America, since it is the first country in the region with a law specifically aimed at the restitution of Indigenous human remains,” Ayala, an archaeologist at the Universidad de Chile, Santiago tells The Art Newspaper. “In Chile, by contrast, there is no legal framework of this kind. That is why it was both necessary and interesting to compare the two realities.”

The researchers’ article, “Indigenous Repatriation Movements in South America and Their Repercussions on Ethical Discussions on the Respectful Treatment of Human Remains: The Cases of Chile and Argentina”, was published on 11 September in the journal Latin American Antiquity. It emerged from Arthur and Ayala’s work with Indigenous communities in Chile, particularly the campaigns led by the Atacameño and Rapa Nui people, where demands for the respectful treatment of human remains include critiques of their scientific study, museum display, sample collection, repatriation and reburial.

Those efforts were underscored last July, when the Australian Museum in Sydney returned the remains of ancestors of the Rapa Nui people who had been removed from sacred burial sites at Rano Raraku during a German naval expedition in 1882, and acquired by the museum the following year. The institution’s director, Kim McKay, publicly acknowledged the circumstances under which the ancestors’ remains had entered the collection, and said: “Returning them is an act of moral responsibility.”

According to Ayala, despite the legal differences between Argentina and Chile, the treatment of human remains from an Indigenous perspective “has not yet become central to scientific concerns”. Indigenous activism, she says, has forced museums and archaeologists to confront “the exclusion of Indigenous voices” and “alternative knowledge and ontologies” linked to ancestral bodies and the materials associated with them. It has also brought renewed attention to the violence of looting, collecting and scientific research that helped shape colonial and national museums, where Indigenous ancestral remains have ended up since at least the 19th century.

“In this context, both museums and academic fields have begun to reflect on their practices and discourses,” Ayala says, “although much work remains to be done to fully integrate the rights of Indigenous peoples in both countries.”

Argentina passed a law in 2001 mandating that Indigenous human remains held in public or private collections must be made available to the peoples or communities that claim them. An implementing decree followed in 2010, making the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs responsible for surveying and identifying remains, and coordinating their return.

A recent case at the Museo Etnográfico Juan B. Ambrosetti, part of the Universidad de Buenos Aires, shows how such restitutions unfold in practice. Last May the museum returned the remains of an Inca child from Apu Chañi, along with his grave goods, to El Angosto and Sol de Mayo, two communities in the El Moreno area of Jujuy state. The child had entered the museum’s collection in 1905, after being brought down from a hill on Nevado de Chañi. Following the restitution, a mausoleum was built at the foot of the mountain to display the grave goods, while the child’s remains will be buried at high altitude when conditions in the freezing high Andes allow.

“What I think is missing here, above all, is getting ahead of restitutions, not waiting for communities to file a claim,” Andrea Pegoraro, the director of the Museo Etnográfico, tells The Art Newspaper. Pegoraro, says the return of the child from Apu Chañi shows that Argentina has a more developed legal framework than many neighbouring countries, but also exposes the limits of a policy based solely on responding to claims.

That, she says, is one of the challenges still facing Argentine museums: moving from responding to specific requests to actively reviewing collections, identifying provenance gaps, reconstructing acquisition histories and contacting the relevant communities. In the Apu Chañi case, she says, the museum reviewed archival and archaeological records to establish where the remains had been taken and to which community they should be returned.

At the restitution ceremony, Pegoraro said the museum was not handing over “a heritage object or an object of study”, but rather “an ancestor to his territory and his people”. The community, in turn, described the returned ancestor as “a guardian” connected to water and life in the Puna region of Jujuy.

For Pegoraro, the distinction between human remains and objects is crucial. “If they are human remains, I am fully in favour of returning them, and the community must decide what to do with them,” she says. Objects raise a different set of considerations, in her view: to whom they should be returned, what happens to them and how museums can ensure access for other communities.

Reconstructing provenance is essential to any restitution process, Pegoraro adds, because Indigenous territories do not always align with today’s political boundaries. “Communities inhabit territories that did not previously have the political or geographical boundaries we have today,” she says. Museums often rely on documentation archaeologists wrote at the time the remains entered a collection, even when the places they recorded no longer correspond neatly to current jurisdictions.

Pegoraro also warns that change cannot be limited to isolated restitutions. “The integration of Indigenous communities does not come only through rhetoric, or by carrying out a restitution or holding an exhibition once in a while, but by literally working side by side,” she says. She adds that collaboration must include the ongoing rewriting of exhibition narratives, as well as financial compensation.

In Pegoraro’s view, the current movement for repatriation of Indigenous remains and artefacts began in the 1980s, especially in the US, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. In Argentina and elsewhere in South America, she adds, those demands gained force with the return of democracy after dictatorships. In Europe, however, museums carry “a much stronger colonial history”, she says, and while some countries are beginning to talk about decolonising collections, returning objects or rewriting narratives, “they still have a long way to go. It must not remain just rhetoric.”

The restituted human remains include 17 skulls and one sample of hair, which were taken from the island during a German expedition in 1882

On public view for the first time, the objects were all returned during outgoing president Gustavo Petro’s administration

The institution intensified its repatriation efforts after revised federal rules governing Native American remains and funerary objects went into effect earlier this year

#9015. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

#9014. Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”

He also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

Denver Design District has unveiled a slick new brand identity, transforming the once exclusive design commerce hub into a fresh cultural destination. A blend of design-focused goods, art, retail and food, the new identity marks a more accessible, culturally relevant district made for the masses.

While there's no formula for creating the best rebrands, Denver Design District's new identity shines in its attention to detail, honouring its rich design heritage while embracing a newfound playfulness. Sleek, timeless and characterful, the new brand identity is the ultimate love letter to design.

Created in collaboration with D4 Urban and design studio Wunder Werkz, the Denver Design District rebrand centres around a wonderfully contemporary brandmark. Representing the district's evolution, the 3 'Ds' motif compresses the bold letterforms by a third each time, making for a dynamic visual anchor.

To accomodate the brandmark, Wunder Werkz created DDD Standard, a bespoke midweight sans serif, to act as the district's display typeface. Equal parts "architectural and playful", it draws inspiration from Herbert Bayer's mid-century furniture forms. Paired with an iconographic system of silhouetted design products, clarity and cohesion flow throughout the identity with a confident authority.

“The idea was to make a more welcoming, accessible district; one that celebrates design in all its forms,” explains Jon Hartman, Partner at Wunder Werkz. “Trade remains an important part of the ecosystem, but it is no longer the whole story. So, we needed to design a brand that felt open and culturally relevant while still carrying the credibility of the design industry.”

A rich colour system of brick, blush, slate and deep yellow contrasts the tans and greys of the district's buildings, bringing warmth and personality to the clean design. The result is a refined homage to design that feels accessible and unpretentious, without losing the slick essence of the design district.

“This project represents the kind of work we love most because it allows us to engage at every level, from strategy and stakeholder alignment through implementation and installation,” adds Hartman. “For us, that’s where the best work happens. Not when design is treated as an afterthought, but when it becomes the link between strategy, space and experience. The result is a brand that feels cohesive at every scale, from a website headline to a warehouse-sized building facade.”

“Denver Design District has always been rooted in great design, but our vision for its future is much broader,” says Dan Cohen, CEO of Denver Design District. “This rebrand isn’t about changing who we are, it’s about reflecting what the District is becoming: a more dynamic, connected, and welcoming destination for Denver and the entire Rocky Mountain region.”

#9011. After nearly two decades, the Old Acropolis Museum in Athens re-opens

Michael Rakowitz, What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026)

Courtesy the artist and Neon. Commissioned by Neon. © Natalia Tsoukala

The Old Acropolis Museum, the first Greek museum to be built in modern times, re-opened on Monday after a major restoration project. It is the first time the museum, founded in 1874 and nestled into the rock of the storied Acropolis hill, has been accessible to the public since 2007.

The opening ceremony was a grand affair, with speeches by the Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and the country’s minister of culture Lina Mendoni, among others.

Once simply the “Museum”, the Old Acropolis Museum took its current name in 2009, when Athens built a newer Acropolis Museum 300 yards down the hill. This offered larger and state-of-the-art space in which to house the antiquities from the Parthenon and other Greek sites, as well as a viewing room designed for the Elgin Marbles—currently showing casts, but with the idea that one day the museum might one day welcome the real items.

The Old Acropolis Museum was left empty for years, and plans eventually developed to use it as storage and administrative spaces. But by 2019, the Greek state definitively nixed this idea.

“For us, it was inconceivable, almost an affront, that this historic building, with its unique location, should be converted into offices and storage facilities,” said Mendoni during her opening speech. “We therefore decided that the museum should reopen in accordance with its original purpose. However, it was not to become just another conventional museum, but rather a museum and exhibition space hosting exhibitions on the history, archaeology and culture of Athens, as well as contemporary art exhibitions inspired by Greek civilisation and innovative programmes incorporating cutting-edge technology.”

The museum will now host both a rotating selection of artefacts as well as a contemporary art programme. The first exhibition, Athens City Idea, focuses on Athens as a social, political, and economic entity, via tragic masks, statues, coins, and amphorae that have been in storage elsewhere across Athens, plus recent discoveries. A digital art component animated the Parthenon’s friezes and the history of the Acropolis Hill.

Part of the idea behind the temporary exhibitions is to keep the museum’s display current, a point also underlined by its commitment to contemporary art.

This includes the last of a trilogy of works commissioned for Athens from the American artist Michael Rakowitz, which is also the final project of Neon, the roving art foundation created by Dimitris Daskalopoulos that for 14 years has funded art and exhibitions across the city, and which announced its closure earlier this year.

“You could say that the first contemporary work here was Phidias’s statue of Athena in the 5th century BCE,” quipped Daskalopoulos, the Athens-born collector who founded Neon. Daskalopoulos also supported the refurbishment of the Old Acropolis Museum, which was funded by both private and public money. “But encouraging the coexistence of antiquity with the contemporary is a challenge we have embraced many times throughout our work at Neon.”

Michael Rakowitz and Elina Kountouri, the director of Neon, outside the reopened Old Acropolis Museum

Rakowitz’s installation What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026), which was commissioned by Neon, and comprises a kiln and newly fired bricks, looks at a lesser-known episode in the Acropolis’s history.

“I realised that you could only tell the whole story of the site if you look through the lens of migration,” the artist told The Art Newspaper. He studied the population exchanges during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, when Greece and Turkey forced a combined total of around 1.5 million inhabitants to leave—Christian Turks to Greece and Muslim Greeks to Turkey. When the Turkish refugees arrived in Athens, they set up tents and encampments at the base of the Acropolis hill.

“Thinking about a ruin as being something that can renew itself to a population and become once again a shelter excited me,” he said. "When I found out about the tradition of the Asia Minor refugees who were able to go back to Turkey after some years, and then the Muslims who were uprooted from Greece, when those populations were able to visit their the departed homelands, they found oftentimes their buildings or towns in a state of ruin, and they would take a brick from that place and bring it back as a memento.”

Installation view of Michael Rakowitz, What You Leave Behind Is Not What Is Engraved (2026)

Courtesy the artist and Neon. Commissioned by Neon. © Natalia Tsoukala

Rakowitz has incorporated these original bricks alongside ones newly made with inscriptions and stamps that bear witness to more recent histories of displacement. For these he worked with survivors of the 1920s population transfers as well as women in the Melissa Network, a nonprofit organisation that supports migrant women in Greece.

“I wanted these bricks to become a foundation for a new kind of city that welcomes strangers and doesn't push them back at sea,” he said.

After sponsoring many exhibitions and commissions across his native Greece, Neon founder Dimitris Daskalopoulos will continue to fund individual projects in Athens and several curatorial posts

Pandermalis, a revered archaeologist and professor, had also been outspoken in calling for the reunification of all the Parthenon marbles in Athens

Athens are still hopeful that the marbles will be returned, to be be housed in the currently unfinished New Acropolis Museum

The Acropolis museum is under construction, and the design for the permanent exhibition is in preparation

#9010. Mason & Fifth's Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact”

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice New-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The company has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice New-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

Just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” said the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth

#9008. Architects and designers celebrate at Dezeen Awards 2026 party in London

Photography by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery

The world’s leading architects and designers from over 40 countries joined to celebrate Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, announcing this year’s winners at a party in London.

More than 550 guests from countries including Angola, Canada and India, as well as Japan, South Africa and Uruguay, joined Dezeen for the event at the historic Royal Opera House in central London.

Guests were welcomed with a champagne reception provided by exclusive drinks partner Veuve Clicquot as they entered the Grade-II listed Paul Hamlyn Hall at the opera house.

The hall’s glazed interior was illuminated and washed in vivid colours drawn from this year’s awards graphic identity in a show design led by Hingston Studio.

Partygoers enjoyed their drinks set against a textile softwall bar backdrop designed by Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen for Canadian studio Molo, known for its sculptural space partitions, furniture and lighting made from paper and textile.

Dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li opened the evening’s ceremony. They welcomed Dezeen’s founding director and board member Rupinder Bhogal to the stage to lead a tribute to the magazine’s founder, the late Marcus Fairs, in honour of its 20th year.

After guests joined in a toast, Hobson and Li then introduced the evening’s keynote speaker, Norman Foster.

The British architect delivered a speech that explored creative and artificial intelligence within the evolving landscape of global architecture. Drawing on his prolific career, the nonagenarian advocated that meaningful innovation requires challenging the status quo.

Dezeen’s editorial director of special projects Max Fraser and awards and events director Claire Barrett then led the evening’s winner announcements.

First to be announced were the design categories, which saw design project of the year awarded to the V&A East’s wayfinding scheme.

Stockholm-based Simon Skinner and British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori were named as this year’s emerging designer of the year and designer of the year, respectively.

Skinner and Ilori won in this year’s Designers of the Year initiative, which recognises the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

Interiors project of the year, sponsored by Gaggenau, went to Barcelona-based Raul Sanchez’s renovation of an old sailor’s home. Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was awarded emerging interior designer of the year, with Tokyo-based Keiji Ashizawa taking the award as this year’s established designer. The interiors project categories were also sponsored by Programa and Framery.

Architecture project of the year was awarded to Daichi’s treetop sauna. The architecture project categories were also sponsored by Michelmersh and Sanderson.

The evening’s presentations culminated with Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect Elsa Escobedo jointly winning emerging architect of the year, while world-renowned practitioner Lina Ghotmeh was named architect of the year.

All the winners received a bespoke trophy made from sustainably harvested cork produced by Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim.

Dezeen Awards winners, VIPs and invited guests continued celebrating into the early hours at an exclusive afterparty sponsored by creative technology studio Made by On at the House of Louie‘s sequestered cocktail hideaway, the Alligator Bar.

All Dezeen Awards 2026 winners were published on Dezeen last Monday evening. Each winner was also featured on a dedicated page on the awards website.

The next edition of Dezeen Awards will open in February 2027. Sign up for the Dezeen Awards newsletter to be the first to hear the latest updates.

The photography is by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

#9007. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

#9006. Ahead of Taiwan local elections, politicians crowd in at Art Taipei

This year's edition of Taiwan's 34-year-old fair Art Taipei (29 October to 2 November) and its third concurrent Taipei Art Week (TAW) fell, serendipitously, just before the alleged spying scandal that emerged around Taiwan's celebrated native son, the naturalised American Nvidia mogul Jensen Huang. This spared fair sales the ensuing worldwide tech stock dive. Rather, concerns during the fair focused more on the pending midterm elections on 28 November.

The fair's opening ceremony was thick with politicians. Prominent figures included incumbent Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an, now in a close re-election race, who would days later face protests at the Taipei Pride parade and festival over his police department's aggressive raid of gay bar Commander D on 3 October. Taiwan's minister of culture Li Yuan heralded his department's successful efforts in September to get a pavilion at the Gwangju Biennale named for Taiwan rather than the sponsoring institution, which sparked a diplomatic row with mainland China, and pronounced that "AI will not replace artists!"

"The presence of political figures at art fairs is a familiar feature of Taiwan's cultural landscape," says Claudia Chen, director of Art Taipei, chair of its organiser, the Taipei Art Gallery Association (Taga), and cofounder of Taipei's Liang Gallery. She adds that it builds public visibility and engagement for the cultural sector. "We hope this attention can help deepen public understanding of the art market and highlight its close connections with cultural development, urban growth, and international exchange."

The question, she continues, "is whether this engagement with political leaders can translate into consistent policy support, particularly in areas such as arts education, international promotion, and incentives for private collecting and cultural patronage." Taiwan lags behind most East Asian governments in cultural investment. "We hope cultural development can become an important public issue and receive sustained support across political parties, allowing Taiwan to gradually translate its economic strength into a deeper and more far-reaching cultural influence."

Chen says that Taiwan's technology sector and the private wealth it fuels "provide an important foundation for its art market. However, translating economic growth into greater activity in the art market takes time," as well as innovation and outreach by galleries.

The 127 galleries that Art Taipei welcomed to the Taipei World Trade Center this year included the return of influential galleries such as Richard Koh Fine Art, from Kuala Lumpur and Singapore, for the first time post-pandemic, and Perrotin for a third consecutive year. Newcomers included Tokyo's Misako & Rosen. One of Taipei's leading platforms, Tina Keng Gallery (TKG+) and TKG+ Projects, joined for the first time in about five years. "In recent years, with Singapore, Seoul, Hong Kong, there is a lot happening, so we needed an opportunity to do a Taiwan show," says the gallery's assistant to the director, Alice Liang. With the suspension of the sleeker international fair Taipei Dangdai after 2025, Art Taipei has resumed its status as the main "hometown" option, she says.

Sales of a "museum-type" installation of works by artists including Sanyu, Kuo Tzumin and Michael Lin went "pretty well", says Liang. "People were surprised and curious," with "positive feedback" from collectors who skewed young and were both Taiwanese and foreign. She adds that the launch of the broader art week had little impact on sales, "but we can feel the difference, with the events, parties and open studios."

Fair organisers also report a generational shift among buyers, with 20.8% of those surveyed saying they were attending for the first or second time, double the figure for 2023. VIP collectors also declined from 77.5% to 54.2%, suggesting that the publicly accessible side of the art week is also providing outreach for the fair. Endeavours included five bus rounds, guided tours, digital art screenings at Taipei Lumitree and 30 public artworks displayed citywide, says Chen. For the art industry, a forum included speakers such as M+ Hong Kong curator Russell Storer and 2026 Venice Biennale Korea Pavilion curator Binna Choi.

The fair also featured an expanded presence of galleries from Korea and Japan, with 25 and 22 respectively, drawing on Taga's ongoing collaboration with those countries' gallery associations. Galleries from Japan, Taiwan's former coloniser, "have maintained a longstanding presence in the Taiwanese market, with many having established strong collector networks and brand recognition over the years," says Chen. The Korean presence "demonstrates the Korean art industry's capacity to expand into international markets through collaboration."

Tastes at the fair are also shifting towards Pop and contemporary art, says dealer Steven Chen (no relation). His Taipei gallery Yiyun Art has attended the fair for seven of the past ten years. It represents traditional Asian paintings, which remain a major sector at Art Taipei, if reduced from previous years. His dramatic maze of a booth, evoking a Chinese scholar's garden, saw steady crowds and sales, including of a painting by Yu Cheng Yao for $90,000. "With the young generation is coming more to the fair," says Chen, "we need a new language on ink art. It is the same culture with a new expression."

Claudia Chen says that Taiwan's collectors are maintaining "purchasing momentum" but have become increasingly deliberate, needing time and established relationships with galleries. Meanwhile, younger collectors are "gradually entering the market, bringing more diverse perspectives shaped by their own lifestyles and aesthetic preferences."

#9005. Raúl Sánchez Architects transforms laundry into light-filled Barcelona home

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.

Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for new solutions to add more light.

“Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight,” studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a “modern translation of the old wells” that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house’s upper level.

The 40-square-metre lower level houses an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area, a bathroom and a small study.

This can be partitioned off from the living space using folding doors made from wood and rice paper, inspired by the clients’ time living in Japan.

In the kitchen, Sánchez said he added a mirror-clad island to “introduce a sense of fragility without disrupting the open feel of the space”.

The upper level, meanwhile, houses the home’s bedrooms and a bathroom. The two floors are connected by the Klein-blue lightwell, which has oculi on all four sides to help distribute the illumination from its skylight throughout the space.

Sánchez wanted to “bring that picturesque atmosphere of Aiguafreda Street into the house, making it part of its surroundings by reclaiming that well – now translated into a lightwell that also helps regulate the home’s temperature.”

This was one of many tailor-made solutions to turn the former laundry house into a home.

“There were many challenges, both technical – access to the mezzanine level, the new staircase, the structural reinforcements – and functional, like fitting the program into just 80 square metres,” Sánchez said.

His studio also worked with materials that would complement the existing ones, using terracotta tiles on the ground floor to extend the traditional exterior clay paving and adding colored glazed tiles to the washbasins and bathroom walls.

“Ultimately, the goal is always to create a cohesive, overarching project that addresses all these challenges and offers something extra – something almost hard to put into words, but that translates into simply feeling good in the space,” Sánchez concluded.

Rául Sánchez Architects is currently working on the final phase of the project, the design of its orchard and garden, which will begin at the start of 2027.

The studio also recently designed a concrete home with a sunken courtyard in Cala Tamarit.

#9003. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

Imagine checking into a Park Hyatt — marble floors, a sommelier who remembers your name by day two, a room that costs $400 a night — and knowing you paid for it with points you earned by writing your rent check. Not by flying 100,000 miles. Not by spending on a business credit card. By paying the bill you were already going to pay anyway. That's the emotional core of this sweet spot, and it's one of the most powerful entry points into travel rewards for the ChooseFI community. Rent is typically your single largest monthly expense, and for years it was a dead end — money out the door with zero return. Bilt Rewards changed that equation entirely. Here's the math that should stop you mid-scroll: a single night at a Category 4 Hyatt — think Hyatt Place in a major city or a solid Park Hyatt property in a secondary market — costs around $150–$250 in cash. With World of Hyatt points, that same night runs 15,000 points. Transfer your Bilt points at a 1:1 ratio, and you've just redeemed at roughly 1–1.7 cents per point at the low end. But at a Category 6 or 7 property — a Grand Hyatt in Tokyo, a Alila in Bali, an Andaz on the Sunset Strip — cash rates climb to $350–$600 per night while the award chart holds steady. That's where you hit **4–8 cents per point**, the upper end of what any hotel currency in the world delivers. The CPP range for this redemption runs **2–8 cents per point**, with a retail value of **$100–$400 per redemption unit**. In loyalty currency terms, that's elite-tier performance. Most hotel points deliver 0.5–0.8 cents. Hyatt points, earned through your rent payment and transferred instantly, routinely deliver 3–5x that value. This is a **pricing inefficiency built into Hyatt's fixed award chart**. Hyatt hasn't aggressively devalued the way other programs have. The chart still prices aspirational properties at points levels that don't reflect their true cash cost — and Bilt gives you a direct pipeline to those points through the expense you can't avoid. For anyone on the path to FI, that's not a hack. That's just math working in your favor.

Why rent-to-hotel is one of the most accessible travel rewards sweet spots

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

The core insight here has two parts, and understanding both will change how you think about every dollar of rent you pay going forward.

Part One: Bilt Is the Only Card That Earns Points on Rent With No Fee

Most landlords don't accept credit cards. Those that do typically charge a 2–3% processing fee, which instantly erases any rewards value. Bilt solved this by partnering directly with property management companies and creating a system where you pay rent via the Bilt app, and the payment processes as ACH (no fee to you or your landlord), while Bilt credits your account with points. You earn 1x point per dollar on rent, up to 100,000 points per year. On a $2,000/month rent payment, that's 24,000 Hyatt points annually from a bill you were paying anyway. Zero incremental spend. Zero fees.

The one rule to know: you must make at least 5 transactions on your Bilt card each statement period to earn points on rent. Five purchases — even five $1 transactions — unlocks the rent earnings. This is a simple, low-lift requirement.

Part Two: World of Hyatt's Fixed Award Chart Is the Unlock

Once your Bilt points are sitting in your account, you transfer them to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant. No waiting 3–5 business days. No points in limbo while availability disappears. You search, you find availability, you transfer, you book — in a single session if you want.

Hyatt's award chart is category-based, fixed pricing from 3,500 points (Category 1) to 45,000 points (Category 8) per night. This is the inefficiency. When a Park Hyatt in a major international city costs $500 in cash but only 30,000 points (Category 6), you're extracting 1.67 cents per point at minimum — and in peak season when cash rates hit $700, you're at 2.3+ cpp. The chart doesn't move with cash prices.

What makes this particularly powerful for the ChooseFI community is the no fuel surcharges policy — Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award stays, so 15,000 points always means exactly 15,000 points out of your account. No surprise $75 "carrier fees" tacked on at checkout.

The transfer path is: Bilt Rewards → World of Hyatt at 1:1, instant. Chase Ultimate Rewards also transfers to Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, which means if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you have a second pipeline to the same program — an important redundancy for maximizing this sweet spot.

For 5,000 points — a single night at a Category 1 or 2 property — you're looking at a $100–$150 night that might cost you 2.5 months of coffee purchases on the Bilt card. That's the entry point. The ceiling is a $400+ night at a Category 5–7 property for 20,000–30,000 points. Both ends of the spectrum represent exceptional value, which is rare in any loyalty program.

Head to biltrewards.com and apply for the Bilt Mastercard (issued by Wells Fargo). The card has no annual fee. Once approved, add the card to your Bilt app and register your rent payment. If your building is in the Bilt Alliance (a growing network of partnered properties), setup is seamless. If not, you can still pay rent through the Bilt app via ACH transfer — Bilt mails a check to your landlord on your behalf, and you still earn points.

Key setup rule: Activate rent rewards in the app before your first payment cycle.

Before rent points post, you need five qualifying purchases on your Bilt card that statement period. Set up small recurring charges — a streaming subscription, a coffee shop, a weekly grocery run — and you'll hit this automatically. Don't forget this step; missing it means forfeiting that month's rent points.

Go to world.hyatt.com and use the award availability search. Select "Use Points" and search your destination and dates. Hyatt's search shows availability up to 395 days in advance — one of the longest windows in the hotel loyalty space. Identify your property, confirm the points price and availability, then — and only then — proceed to transfer.

Never transfer points without confirmed availability. Even though Hyatt availability is generally strong, you want to lock in what you see before moving irreversible points.

In the Bilt app, navigate to "Redeem" → "Transfer Points" and select World of Hyatt. Enter the exact number of points you need. The transfer is instant — points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes, not days. This is one of Bilt's most underrated features and means you can act on last-minute availability without risk.

Return to world.hyatt.com, confirm your points balance has updated, and complete your booking. You'll pay zero fuel surcharges — the points cost is the only cost. You can also call the World of Hyatt reservations line if you need help with a complex booking or want to stack a free night certificate.

If your first-choice property is sold out on points, try these tactics:

Hotel loyalty programs use "award charts" that assign each property a category level with a fixed points price. When a hotel's cash rate rises due to demand or location, the points price stays the same. This creates the value gap that makes points redemptions worthwhile. Hyatt's chart is considered the most generous among major hotel chains because it has resisted the aggressive devaluations that Hilton and Marriott have implemented. A Category 7 property might cost $500-$800 per night in cash but only 30,000 points. That gap is where your 4-8 cents per point value comes from.
