#8985. Meet Courage Dzidula Kpodo, Lesley Lokko's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated

Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will “help shape the next chapter of African architecture”.

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a “linear prescription of urbanisation”.

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is currently using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would “preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account,” Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

“The committee at MIT was a bit shocked, because they weren’t used to the idea of a thesis project existing in the real world,” Kpodo told Dezeen. “But I still thought of it as almost as a sort of sketch, just at 1:1 scale.”

“Doing that gives you something to test – people are going to interface with it; you can test out its failures and success very quickly.”

Growing up in Kumasi, Kpodo initially focused on visual art in school before pursuing a course in architecture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), and subsequently MIT.

At KNUST he was quickly exposed to narratives around both architectural success and Ghana’s own architectural history that left him seeking something more “homegrown”.

“We had a lecture from Francis Kéré in which he spoke about his Serpentine Pavilion, and how taking on commissions from big institutions or big clients can become critical for defining your practice,” said Kpodo.

I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come?

“At the time, I couldn’t imagine any of these commissions coming to those of us working in the South. I couldn’t see any architects who were operating on that scale, or even at a kind of global scale,” he continued.

“It almost had the opposite effect on me. I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come? I think it’s by being local that I can have something to offer to the world.”

Kpodo became interested in local architectural archives, initially those of the KNUST Development Office, but also the less formalised collections of images and drawings that he encountered online.

He soon helped establish Postbox Ghana, a research collective initiated by artist Manuela Nebuloni to create an alternative architectural archive using postcards and stamps from the 1950s to the 1980s, which often depicted examples of Tropical Modernism and state infrastructure constructed following Ghana’s independence.

However, Kpodo still felt that these archival materials did not speak to his own understanding of Ghanaian architecture, having grown up in a “not-so-well-to-do context” in Kumasi and only really encountering modernist architecture when first entering the KNUST campus.

“The whole archive that I was exposed to, whether it was in the Development Office or in the postcards, had a huge, significant gap in it,” he said. “I remember stories my dad would tell me about building practices and cultures that just didn’t make it into this archive or our training in architecture school.”

“As a newly independent country, Ghana wanted to break away from any kind of ethnographic notion of what the ‘Gold Coast’ – to use its colonial name – was. So those ‘traditional’ buildings and other forms of practices did not make it into the framework of thinking about what our future meant,” he continued.

“But even though these buildings are far removed from the city centres and from the archive, they were foundational in the sense that they enabled the cocoa industry, and brought in the money that built the institutions and structures that are enshrined in postcards.”

Kpodo began to photograph these vernacular buildings himself, many of them farm structures made using laterite, a type of local red earth that is formed into air and sun-dried blocks for construction

When I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’

Upon finding many of these buildings slated for demolition, Kpodo has more recently begun to purchase them, before carefully deconstructing their laterite structures to become the raw material for new structures on his land.

The idea was initially met locally with some confusion. “I remember one man said, ‘oh, are you going to extract gold from the walls?’ because laterite can contain gold,” he recalled.

“But when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’ And then some kids would even begin making their own proposals. For me, just creating that imagination is worth it.”

The land that Kpodo purchased in 2022 is in Ghana’s eastern region, and was at the frontier of cocoa production in the early 1900s. Some descendants of the first farmers on the land are still based there, and were among those Kpodo interviewed to understand the history of the landscape.

Alongside the widening of a communal path – the focus of his MIT thesis – and the moving of vernacular building materials there, he has also constructed a simple timber deck, both as a rest point for the farmers and an observation point for watching future changes unfold on the site.

If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too. You can only do so much in an exhibition setting

Kpodo envisions that this future will include both new agricultural processing facilities for the farmers on the land, as well as community spaces that enable further discussions around its ongoing development.

This work also forms the basis of Kpodo’s educational and curatorial work. He is keen to continue “speaking both languages” – the more practical with the conceptual – but he feels the latter should always be grounded in a “local base” rather than detached from it.

In 2023, his work with Postbox Ghana was exhibited at both Vantage Point Sharjah and the Venice Architecture Biennale. In 2025, he curated the LagosPhoto Biennial alongside Maria Pia Bernardoni and Robin Beth Riskin, with the theme of Incarceration.

Kpodo also taught on the one-month Nomadic African Studio at the African Futures Institute, founded by Lokko as a space “dedicated to rethinking education, culture, and practice from the African continent outward.”

Most recently, he orchestrated the transportation of the wall of a laterite farmhouse a little further afield to the Fondation Cartier in Paris, as part of the exhibition Ibrahim Mahama: Harvest Season, where it is accompanied by images from the Postbox Ghana archives.

“If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too,” he said. “You can only do so much in an exhibition setting. You can only talk so much. If the work has no ground and no local base, then I think it becomes very difficult for you to bridge what it is that you’re presenting versus the work that it proposes to be doing.”

“We need to cultivate other sites that do the real work, sites that translate it into something which is not necessarily concerned with an educated audience,” he continued.

“My sense is that we’re increasingly going to see the most ‘powerful’ institutions seek out these hyper-local narratives and projects as a way to really understand the world.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#8984. Final Report Details Minor, But Visible Damage to the Bayeux Tapestry Following Trip to the British Museum

A final report released by France’s ministry of culture yesterday details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained some minor damage following its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, reports Le Figaro.

While the overall state of the nearly 1000-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, who co-authored the report, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened, prior to the voyage. News of an initial condition report about the tapestry showing some damage made headlines in September, but this is the first time a final copy has been seen by the media. Related Articles British Museums Are Experiencing a 'Bayeux Bounce' in Attendance, Thanks to Replicas of the Tapestry Scientists Say They've Rediscovered How the Romans Made the British Museum's Color-Shifting Lycurgus Cup

ARTnews has reached out to France’s Ministry of Culture for a copy of the report, which was not shared via press release or posted on its website, as is customary with public announcements.

In other details, translated from the French news story, experts reportedly observed that “a red wool thread in an embroidered area and another from the linen background cloth have undergone a slight progression.” Additionally, they spotted “slight folds and pockets,” as well as areas of tension in the embroidery and its linen support. For the latter, the tapestry’s horizontal display, in contrast with its previous vertical hang, should help fix the stretching issue. The report also warns of areas to watch closely, particularly on the tapestry’s return trip to France in July 2027. These include several more pronounced folds, areas of wear, and a broken thread.

The authors, who conducted their report in July and August, added that it’s not possible to know precisely when the changes occurred within the time span of the tapestry’s transfer from Bayeux to its current display in London. Additionally, they noted that this last check, including additional, highly detailed photographs of the artifact, is the most complete review of the tapestry to date. It was compared with two less thorough assessments made in 2020 and 2025.

“We now know the condition of the tapestry as never before, which will be useful later on,” said Delphine Christophe, general director of heritage in France, speaking to Le Figaro. She added that the overall assessment, despite the noted damage, proved “exceptional,” given the fragile tapestry’s roughly 230-foot length and 20-inch height.

The loan of the tapestry was heavily criticized in the months leading up to the handoff, due to risks of harming it. But after three failed attempts to secure a loan, it was ultimately made possible thanks to a carefully controlled ground transportation plan that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations, aided by the political will of French President Emmanuel Macron. The latter was intent on making a strong diplomatic statement of friendship with the UK. In exchange, France will receive the Sutton Hoo archaeological ship burial and the Lewis Chessmen set from the British Museum. However, as Le Monde’s Roxana Azimi pointed out, “the Sutton Hoo treasure does not resonate at all with the French public,” and the French people “are getting objects that are certainly valuable, but not very impressive.”

As for the Bayeux Tapestry, it is believed to have been made in Canterbury following the coronation of William the Conqueror as king of England in 1066. It tells his side of the Norman Conquest, which was one of the most pivotal moments in English history. Meanwhile, British Museum director Nicolas Cullinan responded frankly to Azimi’s point in Le Monde. “Yes,” he said. “It’s very hard to beat the Bayeux Tapestry.”

#8983. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

The pricing inefficiency occurs when Partner A prices Partner B's premium cabin at a different rate than Partner B charges through its own program. Virgin Atlantic maintains a fixed partner award chart that prices ANA business class at 90,000 miles regardless of demand or seasonality. ANA's own dynamic pricing can push award costs significantly higher during peak periods. This arbitrage between partner pricing and the operating airline's own program is the foundation of most airline travel rewards sweet spots.

## Why This Redemption Is Rated Moderate This isn't a beginner redemption, but it's absolutely within reach for someone who understands the basics of transferable points programs. Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. ANA doesn't release large blocks of partner availability, and what they do release on prime routes like JFK–NRT goes quickly. This is the single biggest obstacle. **The fix:** Search at exactly 331 days out, use United.com for the most accurate availability search, and have flexibility in your travel dates by at least one week in either direction. ### Challenge 2: The Multi-Program Booking Process You're searching on one airline's website (United), transferring points from a bank program (Chase/Amex) to a third airline's loyalty program (Virgin Atlantic), and then booking through that third airline's portal. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. #8981. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

#8980. "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha

Kaleidoscopic patterns adorn the exterior of this pavilion in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio Selldorf Architects as an art gallery.

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei.

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter’s own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with Selldorf Architects as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

“My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,” said Richter.

“The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips,” he continued. “Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project’s context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a “profound culmination of many years of [Richter’s] research into abstraction”.

“I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind,” she said.

“This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness,” she continued.

“The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience.”

Inside, Richter’s paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing. In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that “what matters is I know why we did things”.

#8979. German Museum Transforms Permanent Collection Galleries into Gym to Attract Youth

We’ve seen dance and musical performances in museums, as well as yoga classes, but a full array of gym equipment and gear? Beginning earlier this month and running through February 21, 2027, the Kunstpalast in Düsseldorf, Germany, has set up weight machines, mats, treadmills, ellipticals, and all manner of gym equipment in its permanent exhibition galleries, so that visitors can work out beside the historic and contemporary artworks, reported the Times of London. Whether or not participants are able to take in the art hanging in front of them while bench pressing, is anyone’s guess, but the idea has its fans, some of whom show up to the museum appropriately dressed in workout clothes. Related Articles Museum Wiesbaden Will Be Germany's First Institution to Return Colonial-Era Human Remains to Indonesia The Netherlands and Germany Agree to Return 2,000 Artifacts to Ghana

What artworks do these health-conscious visitors get to enjoy while sweating away? The program titled “Gym. Fit with Art” unfolds across 20 stations beside the museum’s collection of over 800 works, which span pieces by Peter Paul Rubens to Gerhard Richter. It was conceived as a tribute marking the centenary of the GeSoLei, which was the largest trade fair held during the Weimar Republic, which was also dedicated to health.

“We want to target people who might prefer going to the gym rather than a museum on weekends,” and this particularly includes younger audiences, said Alina Fuchte, who has led the project. To wit, “the museum is transforming its collection into an extraordinary fitness circuit,” states the museum website. “Instead of just strolling from painting to painting and admiring the art, visitors will soon be able to get active,” it adds. The endeavor is sponsored by TARGOBANK in cooperation with Technogym, which makes fitness equipment, according to the website.

“Anyone who would rather simply take in the art is equally welcome,” continues the website. This, however, begs the question of whether that simple act may be tough to do while standing beside someone jogging on a treadmill in front of large busts of Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, and his wife, Anna Maria Luisa de’Medici, per just a few examples of the works on view.

One visitor, Kai Heimes, 25, tells the Times of London, “It’s cool to work out in the collection,” and if it feels “awkward” for some, “I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he added.

However, another, Moritz Rossmanith, 40, admitted to being “a bit confused by it all.” Rossmanith was visiting from Rome, and thought it was “very strange to see kids holding thick barbells while there’s old Italian art on the wall.” Children are reportedly the biggest fans of the gym gear.

As for bringing water bottles to the museum-gym, given that many other museums sternly scold visitors for taking covert sips of water inside art galleries, that rule doesn’t seem to apply here.

“Coming here and realizing this is also a space for me, I can feel comfortable here, I can be free here, I can try new things—that, for me, is the first step,” said Fuchte.

Did we mention there is also a range of scheduled fitness classes at the museum? You can sign up here.

#8977. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#8976. Russia Is Erasing Memories of the Gulag and Reframing Stalin’s History

All over Russia, memories of the Soviet Union and its former dictator Joseph Stalin are being manipulated to tell a new story by the government of President Vladimir V. Putin. An investigative report by The New York Times details how the horrors of Gulag camps are being reframed to depict the Soviets as the victors of World War II and the fight against Nazism. Russia is also using the memory of WWII to act as an extension of its fight against Ukraine.

Efforts to rewrite the story of Russia were already in play before the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022. Notably, Memorial, an organization dedicated to memorializing the camps, was dissolved and labelled an “extremist organization” by Russia’s Supreme Court, forcing the group to move its operations abroad. Memorial was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2022. Related Articles EU Countries Renew Call To Exclude Russia from Venice Ahead of 2027 Architecture Biennale Russian Teenager Detained After Posting Neo-Nazi Threats on TikTok, Targeting Moscow Museum

The Gulag was established by Vladimir Lenin in the late 1910s and early 1920s, but Stalin was the one who expanded the operation from the 1920s to the early 1950s. Nearly 1.5 million people were imprisoned in the Gulag and died from extreme cold, starvation, disease, and intense labor. Monuments that preserved its painful history are now being erased or censored. Examples include the shuttering of Moscow’s Gulag Museum earlier this year and the disappearance of at least 26 memorials dedicated to Gulag victims since 2022.

Additionally, in the summer, a Gulag memorial plaque was removed from the Arctic village Yur-Shor, and more symbols of the Gulag are starting to vanish. Under the power of the Kremlin, Russia is undergoing its own modern-day “digital gulag,” according to the Independent. To wit, a mandate now requires that all new digital devices be equipped with the messenger app Max, launched last year by the Russian tech company VK, which allows Russia’s Federal Security Service access to materials from the app.

#8975. Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week

A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen’s US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of NYCxDesign, announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

While BDNY and high-end showcase Salon Art + Design have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers Ross Lovegrove, Karim Rashid and Rem D Koolhaas for a talk moderated by New York-based design writer Camille Okhio.

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows.

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.

This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

Among these was the Brussels-founded design fair Collectible. For its third New York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a former movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities related to WSA.

While the space fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, somewhat chaotic, with one exhibitor staff member being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head as the exhibitors were installing it in their booth.

Collectible called it an “isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor’s equipment”.

“The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously,” a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.

“Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately.”

However, the fair also had some strong showings. Philadelphia-based Dudd Haus showed a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by Jordan Maurice and a paravent made with telephone cords by Overt Cove.

Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by Upstate New York gallery Freaks, and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by Iitem studio.

The fair’s scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators Alex Tieghi-Walker and Lynette Nylander designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki for Objekt Gallery and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by Small Things Studio for Salon 21.

At Collectible, Montreal design collective Ensemble showcased its members’ work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

This was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to Yabu Pushelberg’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including new lamps by Zebulon Perron, sculptural glass lamps by Alex Joncas, metal works by Jérémy Paguet, leather lamps by Jeta Studio and brass-lined mirrors by Jeremy Le Chatelier.

It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.

At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based Zarolat’s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and Polybion, while New York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, Bossa Furniture, showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

BDNY was, as usual, where most of the actual commerce took place during the week. While the interior designers and architects descended on the sample-forward showing, a few brands showed stand-out collections, including Sancal’s showing of Júlia Esqué’s playfully fringed armchairs and Santa & Cole’s modern, fun lighting.

Later in the week, LA-based Basic Space, run by the organisers behind Design Miami, returned to SoHo. With artistic direction by Alexander May, the stark, white-cube approach differed from the in-situ, multi-room afair that characterised the first New York Basic Space in 2025.

The fair featured a focus on big names and multiple co-curators competing for attention on the promotional materials and in the execution.

Standout pieces included the live-edge wood furniture with small metal connective elements by Brooklyn-based designer Gregory Beson, as well as Daniel Swarilov’s metal credenzas, in a section curated by Marquel Williams.

Paris-based Harry Nuriev created a metallic take on first-class airline seats as a standalone installation. Another booth featured an oversized sofa by NFL player Stefon Diggs’ luxury furniture brand Si Vis Pacem, illustrating the fair’s mix of design with celebrity culture.

Finally, Mexico City-based creative studio Fábrica, run by artist Darryl Richardson and partner Maryah Ananda, held its La Sala showcase in a loft near Penn Station.

With a focus on international Black designers, the showcase featured art and design, with the space shaped like a living room by interior designer Johnathan Bailey.

Furniture pieces of note included a slim metal chair by Kai Avent-deLeo and an armchair by Mark Grattan.

The social focus of the event gave it an aesthetic heft, and a few of its stated goals, “community over curation” and “warmth over spectacle”, made it stand out from many of the other offerings from the week.

Judging by the willingness of the different fall fairs to join in, it seems likely that the November design week will fully take off.

#8973. Hoor Al Qasimi Named Curator of 2028 Venice Biennale, Report Details Limited Damage to Bayeux Tapestry Following Transport to the British Museum, and More: Morning Links for November 27, 2026

To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

THE PRINCESS AND THE VENICE BIENNALE. Sheikha Hoor Al Qasimi has been named curator of the 2028 edition of the Venice Biennale, the world’s largest recurring art exhibition, which runs from April 8 to November 26, 2028, ARTnews reports. Al Qasimi is also president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation, a member of the United Arab Emirates’s Sharjawi royal family and president of the Sharjah Museums Authority. She will be the first Arab curator of the Venice Biennale, and was selected upon the recommendation of its president, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco. In a statement, Al Qasimi said: “For me, La Biennale continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators. I am honored to have been invited to curate this exhibition and grateful to President Pietrangelo Buttafuoco and the board for their confidence and trust.” Related Articles Nick Cave, Indian Pavilion Honored in 2026 Venice Biennale Awards, Smithsonian Secretary Responds to Leaked Plans, Marianne Boesky to Open Paris Gallery, and More: Morning Links for November 25, 2026 South African Artist Tamlin Blake Found Dead, Germany to Restitute Archive of Nazi-Persecuted Jehovah's Witnesses to Family, and More: Morning Links for November 24, 2026

DAMAGE REPORT. A report made public yesterday by France’s ministry of culture details where the Bayeux Tapestry sustained damage during the course of its transfer from Normandy to the British Museum, Le Figaro reports. While the overall state of the 950-year-old tapestry was deemed “satisfactory” by the eight conservationists and experts working in France and England, they found there were “two zones of fiber breakage,” new folds and tensions, as well as “very small” damage that appeared in areas that were already weakened before the voyage. The loan of the fragile tapestry was heavily criticized for risking damage to the artifact, but was ultimately made possible in part thanks to carefully controlled ground transport that was designed to eliminate almost all vibrations. The artifact has since become the hottest museum show in London, attracting long lines and selling out tickets within minutes.

A painting recently attributed to Titian, thought to be a self-portrait and purchased for nearly $70,000 in 2024, is on sale in a London gallery for £1.5 million ($1.97 million), and it is among several rediscovered paintings in an exhibition titled Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, open until December 18. [The Art Newspaper]

Two illuminated manuscripts and three crosses from the 15th century were returned from the American collection of Robert McCarthy to Ethiopia, as part of a unique new partnership between the Ethiopian Heritage Authority (EHA), the Toledo Museum of Art (TMA) and McCarthy. [The Voice]

Veruschka, the German supermodel, who became an iconic muse to the fashion, arts and cultural world of the 1960s and 70s, has died at 87. [WWD]

Neil Simmons, a sculptor whose famous marble piece depicting Margaret Thatcher was decapitated by a protester, has died at 73. [The Times of London]

A rare “Breast Bowl,” or “jatte-téton,” that belonged to French Queen Marie Antoinette and was used in her royal “pleasure dairy,” hammered in Paris for $3.23 million with fees, beating its high estimate of $2.19 million. [ARTnews]

The Princess of Wales, spent time at the Hugo Burge Foundation in Berwickshire, which supports the arts in the UK, and she spoke about the healing qualities of art-making with painter Siobhan McLaughlin, who makes her own pigment and works with stone and earth. [Times of London]

KANALIZING. On Saturday, Kanal or Kanal-Centre Pompidou, Brussels’ nearly 10-acre “city-museum,” opens to the public, heralding the Belgian capital’s first major modern and contemporary art museum organized in collaboration with the Centre Pompidou. As ARTnews reported in September, the mega-project of free and ticketed spaces has been met with controversy over the course of its decade in the making, notably because of ongoing uncertainty about its financial survival, its cost, as well as its dependence on the Pompidou in Paris. Unless there is a political turnabout, Kanal’s publicly funded budget allocated by the Brussels-Capital Region is expected to drop from its current €28 million to €10 million by 2029, which is not enough to keep the project running, according to its leaders. This week, at a large press conference attended by ARTnews, Boris Dilliès, the minister-president of the Brussels region, was on the defensive about the initiative, he said he has faith, while admitting to heavy criticism. The story of Kanal’s rocky road to becoming reality has been widely reported in stories pegged to this week’s opening, but few have offered their thoughts on the 10 exhibitions debuting with it, and what it’s like to wander the vast halls of this new cultural phenomenon. ARTnews stayed on to more fully experience the myriad of shows open to previewing guests, which, over the course of two days, included artists and about 5,000 local schoolchildren. Watch this space to hear our take on Europe’s latest, highly ambitious cultural endeavor, including where it already shines, and where there is room – literally, a whole lot of space – for much more still to come.

#8972. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#8971. Studio Gang completes women's leadership campus in Wisconsin

Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women’s conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site’s oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women’s Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and “ideate solutions to complex issues within their industries”.

“Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren’t designed with them in mind,” said the center’s founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. “I wanted to build one that was.”

Studio Gang said key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

“We designed the Women’s Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive,” said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

“Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings’ carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site’s ecology and enhance its biodiversity.”

The campus contains three main buildings — the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.

White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to “reflect the tones and textures of the forest”, according to the studio.

The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.

A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

It also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building’s green roof contains a “coffee nook” and patios for seating.

Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.

Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.

Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.

Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate New York and a Denver hotel.

#8969. Keira Knightley’s Emerald-Green ‘Atonement’ Gown Heads to Christie’s

The stunning emerald-green plunging-back gown worn by actress Keira Knightley in Atonement will be auctioned live in London on December 9 at Christie’s. It is estimated to fetch between £100,000 and £120,000 ($130,940 to $157,125). In addition, the sale titled Love & Lust: A Literary Guide, will offer a host of items “celebrating the many expressions of love, romance and desire,” per the auction house’s description. This will range from passionate letters and cinematic costumes behind famous romances played out on stage and in literature, including about 30 books, manuscripts, autographed letters and original works dating back centuries. Related Articles Christie's Adds UK Auction House Dreweatts to Its Portfolio Yoshitomo Nara Painting Fetches $15.9 M., Outselling Koons and Richter in New York

Knightley wore the silky green ensemble designed by Jacqueline Durran for her role as Cecilia Tallis in the 2007 film Atonement, adapted from Ian McEwan’s acclaimed novel, and directed by Joe Wright. The dress last went under the hammer in a charity auction in 2008 and fetched £35,000 ($46,000).

Also for sale are rare examples of early film poster art, including one of the influential film Metropolis, made in 1926 for its premiere, estimated at £100,000 to £130,000 ($130,940 to $170,220). Another poster for Dracula (1931), which marked a pivotal moment for early sound movies, is being offered for an estimated £80,000 to £120,000 ($104,750 to $157,125).

These lots are joined, among others, by early 19th-century love letters from the celebrated British Royal Navy officer Horatio Nelson to Emma, Lady Hamilton, estimated at £5,000 and £8,000, plus original sketches by Chris Foss for the publication of The Joy of Sex (1972), estimated at £6,000 to £8,000.

“Love and desire have inspired some of the most enduring stories in literature and art, and this sale brings together a wonderfully eclectic group of objects that capture their many facets…” jointly stated Thais Hitchins, associate specialist, and Mark Wiltshire, specialist, Christie’s London.

#8968. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#8967. Thermory Design Awards 2026 recognises striking examples of architecture and design using thermowood

A contemporary take on Ukrainian vernacular buildings and a preschool in Estonia are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified wood.

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to Thermory.

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio YOD Group.

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior’s traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure’s openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” said Thermory.

Winning in the tiny and private house category was Marker Architecture‘s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting,” it added.

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio Arhitekt Must‘s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio AERIS.

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” said Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at Henning Larsen; Sami Rintala, professor and architect at Rintala Eggertsson Architects; Jaan Port, architect and partner at PIN Arhitektid; and Tõnis Kalve, architect at ByKalve and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, visit its website.

The one US price drop I have found is at key retailer Loaded (formerly CDKeys): the PS5 and Xbox digital code is $69.99, down from $79.99, or £69.99 £55.79 in the UK, but that's for the digital edition (okay, they're all digital, but there's no box to collect).

Prefer to buy straight from the PlayStation Store? Discounted gift cards are the workaround. Newegg has about $5 off $70 PSN cards, and promo code BFF3538 takes $25 off $250 cards.

Or UK readers can head to Amazon and get the same £5 off GTA 6 on PlayStation 5, now £69.99 £64.95, without the PSN workaround.

Sony has no official GTA 6 console bundle, and it raised US PS5 prices on April 2: the Slim Digital now lists at $599.99, the Slim with a disc drive at $649.99, and the PS5 Pro at $899.99, so keep these numbers in mind if you see a console and GTA 6 bundle deal. Couple that with Microsoft saying Xbox Series X/S won't be discounted, and you need to watch any bundle deals.

For example, the only US console-plus-GTA 6 package I've found is a PS5 Slim with GTA 6 and an accessories kit at Walmart: $929.99, down from $999.99. Best Buy lists the same bundle at $1,199.99. It saves $70 on paper, but the price is high compared to buying the pieces separately, so check exactly what's in the listing first.

The good news? The best actual GTA 6 related deals I've found are Amazon's GTA 6 + accessory offers, for PS5 and Xbox, so I've listed them below.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy® Is Your On-Ramp

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy®.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

The more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Plan never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

You need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy® at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy® points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:

Tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

If your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

Let's make this concrete. You and your partner are planning a trip to Japan in the spring — cherry blossom season, the dream itinerary for so many in the ChooseFI community.

The Route: Seattle (SEA) → Tokyo Narita (NRT) on JAL Flight 009, operated by a Boeing 787-9.

The Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

The Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

The meal service features both Western and Japanese options, sake and premium spirits, and attentive crew who seem genuinely delighted to serve you. The 9–10 hour flight to Narita passes in quiet, restful comfort. You arrive refreshed.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Given Alaska's limited transfer partners, the most reliable path to a large Alaska miles balance is the Alaska Airlines Visa Signature card, which regularly offers welcome bonuses of 40,000–75,000 miles.
